name: Mesopotamia
summary: Mesopotamia's civilizations rose and fell in succession along the Tigris and Euphrates: Sumerian city-states gave way to Sargon's Akkadian Empire, then the Sumerian revival under the Third Dynasty of Ur, Hammurabi's Babylon, the Neo-Assyrian Empire centered on Nineveh, and finally the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which fell to Cyrus the Great of Persia in 539 BC.
imageAttribution: Map by Goran tek-en, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of ancient Mesopotamia along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

events.title: Cuneiform Emerges at Uruk
events.body: The world's earliest writing system develops from clay tokens used to record grain and livestock at the city of Uruk, becoming the first script for recording language and law.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A monumental Achaemenid-era cuneiform inscription of Xerxes I, carved into the cliff at Van in eastern Turkey.

events.title: Sargon Founds the Akkadian Empire
events.body: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian city-states and unites them under a single ruler, creating what many historians consider the world's first empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by ALFGRN, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Sargon of Akkad depicted on his victory stele.

events.title: Enheduanna Composes Sacred Hymns
events.body: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, writes hymns to the goddess Inanna that scribes keep copying for centuries, making her the first author in world history known by name.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mefman00, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The alabaster Disk of Enheduanna, showing her performing a religious libation ceremony.

events.title: Gutian Invaders Topple the Akkadian Empire
events.body: Raiders from the Gutian people overrun southern Mesopotamia and end Akkadian rule, plunging the region into roughly a century of fragmented, weakened kingship before Ur-Nammu's revival.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A votive mace head dedicated by La-arab, a Gutian king, now in the British Museum.

events.title: Ur-Nammu Founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
events.body: After centuries of Akkadian and Gutian rule, Ur-Nammu reunites southern Mesopotamia under the city of Ur and issues the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest law code known to survive.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Sémhur and Zunkir, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Third Dynasty of Ur's territorial extent under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.

events.title: Ur-Nammu Begins the Great Ziggurat of Ur
events.body: Ur-Nammu breaks ground on a massive stepped temple platform dedicated to the moon god Nanna, a project his son Shulgi completes -- one of the best-preserved ziggurats surviving from ancient Mesopotamia.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Tla2006, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The reconstructed ziggurat of Ur, built under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.

events.title: Elamites Sack Ur, Ending the Third Dynasty
events.body: An Elamite army captures Ur and its king Ibbi-Sin, extinguishing the Third Dynasty after two decades of territorial collapse and closing the last great flowering of Sumerian civilization.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via the Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Ibbi-Sin, the last king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, enthroned.

events.title: Hammurabi's Code Carved in Stone
events.body: Babylon's king publishes 282 laws on a black diorite stele, one of the earliest surviving law codes governing an entire society.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mbzt, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The front face of the Code of Hammurabi stele, now in the Louvre.

events.title: Hittites Sack Babylon, Ending Hammurabi's Dynasty
events.body: Hittite king Mursili I raids deep into Mesopotamia and sacks Babylon, toppling the First Babylonian Dynasty founded by Hammurabi and opening the way for the Kassites to take the throne.
events.imageAttribution: Map by MapMaster, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Babylonia under the Kassite dynasty that succeeded Hammurabi's fallen dynasty.

events.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh Reaches Its Standard Form
events.body: Scholar-priest Sin-Leqi-Unninni compiles the definitive version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, weaving older Sumerian and Akkadian poems about the legendary king of Uruk into the work that survives today as the world's oldest known epic.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by BabelStone, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Flood Tablet, the eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh, from the Library of Ashurbanipal.

events.title: Adad-nirari II Founds the Neo-Assyrian Empire
events.body: Adad-nirari II's accession launches a newly aggressive phase of Assyrian expansion that grows, over the next three centuries, into the largest empire the world had yet seen.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ningyou, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Assyrian Empire at its territorial extent.

events.title: Sennacherib Destroys Babylon
events.body: After Babylon's king allies with Elam and Assyria's own crown prince is captured and executed, Sennacherib razes the rebellious city and diverts a canal to flood its ruins, declaring the land kingless.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Assyrian bas-relief of armed soldiers from the palace of King Sennacherib.

events.title: Esarhaddon Rebuilds Babylon
events.body: Esarhaddon reverses his father's destruction of Babylon, resettling its people and restoring the Esagila temple and Etemenanki ziggurat in a project his successors will need decades to finish.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Assyrian king Esarhaddon depicted on a commemorative stele from Sam'al, now in the Pergamon Museum.

events.title: Ashurbanipal Builds the Library at Nineveh
events.body: Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembles a vast collection of cuneiform tablets at his capital, creating the ancient world's most systematic library and preserving countless Mesopotamian texts for posterity.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by KeyolTranslater, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of King Ashurbanipal hunting lions, from his palace at Nineveh.

events.title: Nabopolassar Founds the Neo-Babylonian Empire
events.body: A former Assyrian official, Nabopolassar seizes Babylon amid Assyria's succession crisis and is crowned king, launching the revolt that destroys the Neo-Assyrian Empire within two decades.
events.imageAttribution: Map by ܥܘܡܪܐ, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Neo-Babylonian Empire founded by Nabopolassar.

events.title: Nineveh Falls
events.body: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes storms the Assyrian capital, ending the Neo-Assyrian Empire's centuries of dominance over the Near East.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Mu-tamajo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: John Martin's 1829 painting The Fall of Nineveh.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II Rebuilds the Etemenanki Ziggurat
events.body: Nebuchadnezzar II raises Babylon's great ziggurat to a scale later Greek and biblical writers mythologize as the Tower of Babel, cementing Babylon's reputation as the ancient world's most spectacular city.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Jona Lendering, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction drawing of the Etemenanki ziggurat, based on Hansjörg Schmid's research.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II Conquers Jerusalem
events.body: After a lengthy siege, Babylonian forces breach Jerusalem's walls, destroy Solomon's Temple, and deport much of the population -- the start of the Babylonian captivity that Cyrus will later end.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Etemenanki, the great ziggurat of Babylon rebuilt under Nebuchadnezzar II.

events.title: Nabonidus Abandons Babylon for Tayma
events.body: Devoted to the moon god Sin over Babylon's own patron deity Marduk, King Nabonidus withdraws to the Arabian oasis of Tayma for roughly a decade, leaving his son Belshazzar as regent and alienating Babylon's priesthood.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of King Nabonidus before the crescent symbol of the moon god Sin, to whom he was devoted.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.body: Cyrus of Persia captures Babylon without a major battle, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire and folding Mesopotamia into the Achaemenid Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Mezzotint by J. Martin (1831), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons / Wellcome Collection
events.imageDescription: J. Martin's 1831 mezzotint depicting Cyrus the Great's conquest of Babylon.

name: Egypt
summary: Ancient Egypt's civilization ran from Narmer's unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BC through the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms -- each followed by a period of fragmentation and reunification -- to the Late Period's conquest by Persia, then Alexander the Great, and finally the Ptolemaic dynasty, which ended with Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BC.
imageAttribution: Photo by Douwe C. van der Zee, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, the last surviving Wonder of the Ancient World.

events.title: Narmer Unites Upper and Lower Egypt
events.body: King Narmer conquers or absorbs Lower Egypt, uniting the Nile valley under a single ruler for the first time and founding the line of pharaohs that will govern Egypt for the next three millennia.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial carved slate commemorating the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

events.title: Djoser Builds the Step Pyramid at Saqqara
events.body: Pharaoh Djoser's architect Imhotep builds Egypt's first monumental stone structure, a six-tiered pyramid that launches the Old Kingdom's age of pyramid-building.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
events.imageDescription: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, Egypt's first monumental stone structure.

events.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza Is Completed
events.body: Pharaoh Khufu's tomb is finished after roughly two decades of construction, standing as the largest pyramid ever built and the last surviving Ancient Wonder of the World.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Douwe C. van der Zee, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Great Pyramid of Giza, built as Khufu's tomb.

events.title: Old Kingdom Collapses, Egypt Fractures into Rival Dynasties
events.body: Pepi II's exceptionally long reign ends in succession chaos, and central authority collapses as increasingly independent nomarchs carve up the country; Egypt splinters into rival Herakleopolitan and Theban dynasties for more than a century.
events.imageAttribution: Limestone Stela of Tjetji, British Museum, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A limestone stela of the official Tjetji, dated to Egypt's 11th Dynasty during the fractured First Intermediate Period.

events.title: Mentuhotep II Reunifies Egypt, Begins the Middle Kingdom
events.body: After more than a century of division known as the First Intermediate Period, Mentuhotep II defeats his rivals and reunites Upper and Lower Egypt, founding the Middle Kingdom from his power base at Thebes.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Prof. Mortel, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A statue of Mentuhotep II from his mortuary complex at Deir el-Bahri, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

events.title: The Story of Sinuhe Is Composed
events.body: An unknown author writes the tale of Sinuhe, an official who flees Egypt after Amenemhat I's death and eventually returns home in old age; copied for over 700 years afterward, it becomes ancient Egypt's most celebrated work of literature.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Olaf Tausch, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A hieratic papyrus copy of the Story of Sinuhe, now in Berlin's Neues Museum.

events.title: Senusret I Founds the Temple of Karnak
events.body: Pharaoh Senusret I begins construction at Karnak with a shrine to the god Amun, launching a building project that later pharaohs will expand for another two thousand years into Egypt's largest temple complex.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Francis Frith, 1857, public domain (Rijksmuseum), via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The hypostyle hall at Karnak, part of the temple complex begun under Senusret I.

events.title: Senusret III Abolishes the Nomarch System
events.body: Senusret III strips Egypt's hereditary provincial nomarchs of their power, replacing the traditional nome administration with a handful of large districts answering directly to the crown -- a centralizing reform that reshapes how the Middle Kingdom is governed.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by ArchaiOptix, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A granite portrait head of Senusret III, broken from a sphinx statue, now in Munich's Staatliches Museum Ägyptischer Kunst.

events.title: The Edwin Smith Papyrus Is Copied
events.body: A scribe copies out Egypt's oldest surviving surgical treatise, a text that diagnoses and treats 48 traumatic injuries through clinical observation -- inspection, smell, pulse-taking -- rather than incantation, making it one of history's earliest examples of rational medicine.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A page of the Edwin Smith Papyrus, discussing the treatment of facial trauma.

events.title: Seqenenre Tao Rebels Against Hyksos Rule
events.body: Theban ruler Seqenenre Tao opens hostilities against the Hyksos kings occupying northern Egypt; he dies violently, likely in combat, but his war of liberation is carried on by his son Kamose and completed by his grandson Ahmose I.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Flinders Petrie, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The rishi-style coffin of Seqenenre Tao, found in the Deir el-Bahari royal cache.

events.title: Ahmose I Expels the Hyksos, Begins the New Kingdom
events.body: Ahmose I captures the Hyksos stronghold of Avaris, driving the foreign dynasty out of Egypt and founding the 18th Dynasty, which will carry Egypt to the height of its power and territorial reach.
events.imageAttribution: Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A carved head of Ahmose I, founder of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

events.title: Akhenaten Launches Egypt's Religious Revolution
events.body: Pharaoh Akhenaten abandons Egypt's traditional pantheon for the worship of a single sun-disc god, Aten, and builds a new capital at Amarna -- a radical break that his successors will reverse within a generation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5

events.title: Thutmose Sculpts the Nefertiti Bust
events.body: The royal sculptor Thutmose creates a painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti in his workshop at Akhenaten's new capital -- a work that survives more than three thousand years to become one of the most reproduced images of ancient Egyptian art.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Philip Pikart, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Nefertiti Bust on display in Berlin's Neues Museum.

events.title: Tutankhamun Restores Egypt's Traditional Religion
events.body: In the fourth year of his reign, the young pharaoh Tutankhamun reverses his father Akhenaten's religious revolution, ending the exclusive worship of Aten and restoring Amun and Egypt's traditional gods, an act he commemorates on the Restoration Stela.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Roland Unger, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The funerary mask of Tutankhamun, in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

events.title: The Battle of Kadesh
events.body: Ramesses II leads Egyptian forces against the Hittite army of Muwatalli II in one of history's largest chariot battles; both sides claim victory, and the standoff eventually produces the world's earliest surviving peace treaty.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
events.imageDescription: The temple of Abu Simbel, built by Ramesses II, whose reliefs commemorate his campaign at Kadesh.

events.title: Tomb Workers Stage History's First Recorded Strike
events.body: In the 29th year of Ramesses III's reign, the royal tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina down tools and march on nearby mortuary temples when their grain rations fail to arrive -- the earliest documented labor strike in recorded history.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The workmen's village of Deir el-Medina, home to the artisans who staged the strike.

events.title: Psamtik I's Reign Revives Middle Kingdom Artistic Style
events.body: Under Psamtik I, founder of the Saite dynasty, Egyptian sculptors deliberately imitate the style of Middle Kingdom masterpieces from a thousand years earlier -- a conscious archaism that signals the restored, unified monarchy's claim to Egypt's classical past.
events.imageAttribution: Bust of Psamtik I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
events.imageDescription: A bust from a statue of Psamtik I, sculpted in a deliberately archaizing style.

events.title: Necho II Commissions a Nile-to-Red-Sea Canal
events.body: Pharaoh Necho II begins cutting a canal to connect the Nile to the Red Sea, a forerunner of the modern Suez Canal, and according to Herodotus sends a Phoenician fleet on a three-year voyage that circumnavigates Africa entirely -- though he abandons the canal unfinished to fight in Syria.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Keith Schengili-Roberts, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bronze kneeling statuette of a Necho pharaoh, now in the Brooklyn Museum.

events.title: Cambyses II Conquers Egypt for Persia
events.body: The Achaemenid king Cambyses II defeats Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium and crowns himself pharaoh, ending Egypt's Late Period independence and folding it into the Persian Empire as a satrapy.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Mossmaps, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the western Achaemenid Empire, including Egypt after Cambyses II's conquest.

events.title: Amyrtaeus Ends Persian Rule, Restores Egyptian Independence
events.body: Amyrtaeus of Sais leads a successful revolt against Achaemenid Persian occupation, expelling Persian forces from Egypt and founding the short-lived 28th Dynasty -- the last native Egyptian dynasty before Persia's second conquest a generation later.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Aramaic loan contract papyrus dated to the reign of Amyrtaeus, from Elephantine.

events.title: Alexander the Great Conquers Egypt
events.body: Alexander enters Egypt to a welcome as a liberator from Persian rule and is crowned pharaoh at Memphis, ending nearly two centuries of Achaemenid control and setting up the Macedonian Greek Ptolemaic dynasty that follows.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (detail of the Alexander Mosaic)
events.imageDescription: A detail of the Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii, depicting Alexander the Great in battle.

events.title: Ptolemy I Promotes the Cult of Serapis
events.body: Ptolemy I promotes worship of Serapis, a new god blending Egyptian Osiris and Apis with Greek iconography, in a deliberate bid to give his Greek and Egyptian subjects a shared object of devotion.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Roman marble copy of a Greek bust of Serapis, from the Serapeum of Alexandria.

events.title: The Library of Alexandria Takes Shape
events.body: Under Ptolemy I and his son Ptolemy II, Alexandria's Library and adjoining Museum take shape as a state-funded center of scholarship, eventually amassing hundreds of thousands of scrolls and drawing the ancient world's leading scientists and scholars.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by O. Von Corven, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century artistic rendering of the Library of Alexandria's reading room.

events.title: The Lighthouse of Alexandria Is Completed
events.body: After roughly twelve years of construction begun under Ptolemy I, the Lighthouse of Alexandria is completed under Ptolemy II on the island of Pharos, rising over 100 meters to become one of the tallest structures in the ancient world and one of its Seven Wonders.
events.imageAttribution: Drawing by Hermann Thiersch, 1909, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction drawing of the Lighthouse of Alexandria by archaeologist Hermann Thiersch.

events.title: The Rosetta Stone Decree Is Issued
events.body: A congress of priests meeting at Memphis issues a decree honoring the young Ptolemy V, inscribing it in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek on what becomes known as the Rosetta Stone -- the trilingual text that will let scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs two thousand years later.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Hans Hillewaert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Rosetta Stone, on display in the British Museum.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra VII
events.body: Egypt's last active pharaoh dies by suicide after Rome's conquest of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, ending nearly three millennia of pharaonic rule and making Egypt a province of Rome.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Louis le Grand, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Roman marble bust of Cleopatra VII, dated to around the time of her visit to Rome, now in Berlin's Altes Museum.

name: Indus Valley
summary: Village farming communities along the Indus and its tributaries grow into walled settlements by 3300 BC, and by 2600 BC these coalesce into a network of standardized cities -- Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, and dozens more -- sharing brick sizes, city planning, and a still-undeciphered script. Indus traders reach Mesopotamia by sea, but the great cities lose population and long-distance contact around 1900 BC as regional rivers dry up, and by 1300 BC the last localized successor cultures fade out, centuries before any written record explains why.
imageAttribution: Map by Avantiputra7, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Indus Valley Civilization's extent during its Mature Phase (2600-1900 BC).

events.title: Early Farming Villages Rise at Kot Diji
events.body: Walled settlements at Kot Diji, on the Indus's east bank opposite the future site of Mohenjo-daro, adopt the fortification style and pottery traditions that mark the start of the Early Harappan period.

events.title: Standardized Weights Regulate Harappan Trade
events.body: Cubical chert weights following a shared binary-and-decimal ratio system, along with finely graduated ivory and shell rulers, appear in near-identical form across Harappan cities -- consistency scholars read as evidence of a central authority able to enforce common standards.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Nomu420, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Harappan-era weighing scale on display at the National Museum in New Delhi.

events.title: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro Rise
events.body: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro emerge as the Indus Valley's twin great cities, their grid-planned streets, standardized baked-brick sizes, and covered drains opening the seven-century Mature Harappan period.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Muhammad Bin Naveed, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Granary and Great Hall on Mound F at the archaeological site of Harappa.

events.title: A Standardized Script Appears on Seals
events.body: Thousands of carved steatite seals carry a symbol system used widely enough across Mature Harappan cities to suggest formal record-keeping, though without any known bilingual text, the script remains undeciphered today.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Indus Valley seal impression showing a five-character Indus script inscription, in the British Museum.

events.title: The Great Bath Is Built at Mohenjo-daro
events.body: Fitted baked bricks sealed with gypsum plaster and a layer of bitumen waterproof Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, a colonnaded tank most scholars read as a site for ritual purification rather than everyday washing.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Aakashaliraza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The colonnaded Great Bath tank at Mohenjo-daro.

events.title: Terracotta Figurines Spark a 'Mother Goddess' Debate
events.body: Small clay figurines of bejeweled women, common across Harappan sites, lead early excavators to propose a widespread fertility-goddess cult, though many scholars today read the same figurines as children's dolls or ornaments rather than religious icons.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Ismoon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A terracotta female figurine from Mohenjo-daro, wearing a fan-shaped headdress and layered jewelry, once read as a 'mother goddess.'

events.title: Dholavira's Reservoirs Turn a Desert City Water-Secure
events.body: Sixteen or more stone-cut reservoirs, some 7 meters deep and fed by dammed seasonal streams, let Dholavira store enough rainwater to sustain a large walled city through Kutch's long dry spells, among the earliest large-scale water-storage systems known anywhere.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bhajish Bharathan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: One of Dholavira's stone-cut water reservoirs.

events.title: Trade Networks Reach Mesopotamia
events.body: Sargon of Akkad's inscriptions describe ships arriving from Meluhha, most likely the Indus Valley, carrying carnelian beads, ivory, and timber to Mesopotamian ports in exchange for silver, wool, and grain.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Sémhur (base) and Zunkir (derivative), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Middle East in the second half of the 3rd millennium BC, spanning the Akkadian and Ur III periods.

events.title: The 'Dancing Girl' Bronze Is Cast at Mohenjo-daro
events.body: A small bronze figure of a bangled young woman, standing with one hand on her hip, is lost-wax cast at Mohenjo-daro, among the earliest known uses of the technique and a rare survival of Harappan figurative metalwork.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The bronze 'Dancing Girl' statuette from Mohenjo-daro, now in the National Museum, New Delhi.

events.title: The Pashupati Seal Depicts a Horned Deity
events.body: A steatite seal from Mohenjo-daro shows a horned, cross-legged figure encircled by wild animals; excavator John Marshall reads it as a proto-Shiva, a claim later scholars treat as one plausible interpretation among several for the civilization's undeciphered iconography.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of an ancient Indus Valley seal, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Pashupati seal, showing a horned seated figure surrounded by animals.

events.title: The Mature Harappan Cities Begin to Decline
events.body: Population and long-distance trade at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro start to contract as the seven-century Mature Harappan period ends, opening a slower slide into regional fragmentation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Saqib Qayyum, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, a large brick-built pool at the center of the city's citadel, likely used for ritual bathing.

events.title: Cemetery H Culture Marks a Late Harappan Shift
events.body: As Mohenjo-daro is abandoned, a new culture identified by cremation burials in painted urns appears at Harappa's "Cemetery H," with settlement pushing eastward and rice farming replacing the old river-trade economy.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Avantiputra7, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Painted pottery urns from Harappa's Cemetery H period, now in the National Museum, New Delhi.

events.title: The Civilization Fades
events.body: A prolonged drying of the region's rivers drains the water supply that sustained Indus cities, and the last Late Harappan successor cultures fade into isolated regional traditions, centuries before any written record explains their end.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Saqib Qayyum, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of a Buddhist stupa built centuries later atop Mohenjo-daro's citadel mound.

name: Greece
summary: Ancient Greece rose from a loose collection of city-states in the Archaic period, through the Classical age's wars with Persia and each other, to Alexander the Great's Macedonian-led conquests that opened the Hellenistic era -- before falling under Roman control after the Achaean War in 146 BC.
imageAttribution: Photo by Phanatic, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Parthenon, the temple to Athena atop the Acropolis in Athens.

events.title: The First Olympic Games
events.body: City-states across Greece send athletes to Olympia for a festival of competition held in honor of Zeus, beginning a tradition that will continue every four years for over a thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bgabel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of the palaestra (wrestling school) at Olympia, site of the ancient Olympic Games.

events.title: Draco's Harsh Laws Are Written Down
events.body: Athens gets its first written law code under the lawgiver Draco, whose penalties are so severe -- reportedly prescribing death for even minor offenses -- that his name gives us the word "draconian."
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Max Karl Baldamus, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1833 engraved portrait of the Athenian lawgiver Draco.

events.title: Solon Enacts Sweeping Reforms
events.body: Chosen archon amid rising unrest, Solon cancels the debts binding many Athenians into servitude and rewrites the city's law code, opening political participation beyond the old aristocracy for the first time.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sailko, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Roman-era marble bust believed to depict the Athenian lawgiver Solon.

events.title: Cleisthenes Founds Athenian Democracy
events.body: Cleisthenes reorganizes Athens' constitution around ten new tribes cutting across old aristocratic loyalties, laying the groundwork for direct democratic government by its citizens.
events.imageAttribution: Unknown artist, CC BY, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern bust of Cleisthenes, regarded as the father of Athenian democracy.

events.title: The Ionian Revolt Begins
events.body: Led by Aristagoras of Miletus, Greek cities along the Anatolian coast rise up against Persian rule, a six-year rebellion that draws in Athens and Eretria and sets the stage for Persia's invasions of the Greek mainland.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Eric Gaba and MinisterForBadTimes, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the military campaigns of the Ionian Revolt against Persian rule.

events.title: Victory at Marathon
events.body: An outnumbered Athenian army routs the first Persian invasion force on the plain of Marathon, a victory that becomes a defining Athenian legend of citizen-soldiers defending their homeland.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by John Steeple Davis, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An illustration of the Battle of Marathon.

events.title: The Battle of Salamis
events.body: A Greek fleet under the Athenian Themistocles lures Xerxes' much larger Persian navy into the narrow straits of Salamis and destroys it, breaking Persia's second invasion of Greece.
events.imageAttribution: Department of History, United States Military Academy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the Persian advance from Thermopylae to Salamis in 480 BC.

events.title: Construction Begins on the Parthenon
events.body: Under Pericles' building program, work starts on a new temple to Athena atop the Acropolis, designed by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates and overseen by the sculptor Phidias.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Steve Swayne, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Parthenon temple on the Acropolis of Athens.

events.title: Phidias Completes the Statue of Zeus at Olympia
events.body: The sculptor Phidias finishes a 40-foot seated figure of Zeus in gold and ivory for the god's temple at Olympia, a work later counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Quatremère de Quincy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century reconstruction of Phidias's gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus in its temple at Olympia.

events.title: The Peloponnesian War Begins
events.body: Long-simmering rivalry between Athens and Sparta erupts into open war between their respective alliances, a 27-year conflict that will exhaust both sides and end Athens' golden age.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Captain Blood, translated by Kenmayer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the alliances and campaigns of the Peloponnesian War.

events.title: Sparta Installs the Thirty Tyrants in Athens
events.body: Following Athens' defeat in the Peloponnesian War, Sparta imposes a pro-Spartan oligarchy of thirty men who suspend democratic government and carry out a violent purge of political opponents.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving published by Guillaume Rouillé, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century engraved portrait of the Spartan general Lysander, who installed the Thirty Tyrants in Athens.

events.title: Thrasybulus Restores Democracy in Athens
events.body: Democratic exiles led by Thrasybulus defeat the forces of the Thirty Tyrants at Munychia and force the oligarchs to step down, restoring Athens' democratic constitution after less than a year of oligarchic rule.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from Andrea Alciato's Emblemata, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A woodcut depicting Thrasybulus being crowned with an olive garland.

events.title: Athens Puts Socrates on Trial
events.body: A jury of Athenian citizens convicts Socrates of impiety and corrupting the youth and sentences him to death by hemlock, a verdict that becomes a defining test case for the relationship between philosophy and the state.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Jacques-Louis David, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Jacques-Louis David's 1787 painting The Death of Socrates, depicting the philosopher's execution by hemlock.

events.title: Philip II Defeats the Greek Alliance at Chaeronea
events.body: Macedonian forces under Philip II, with his son Alexander commanding the cavalry, crush a coalition of Athens and Thebes, ending the independent city-states' resistance and bringing mainland Greece under Macedonian control.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Kirill Lokshin and Dipa_1965, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of troop positions at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC.

events.title: Aristotle Founds the Lyceum
events.body: Returning to Athens after tutoring Alexander the Great, Aristotle begins teaching regularly at the Lyceum and establishes it as a formal school, launching what becomes known as the Peripatetic tradition of philosophy.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Raphael, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A detail from Raphael's The School of Athens depicting Plato and Aristotle.

events.title: Alexander Invades the Persian Empire
events.body: Leading a mostly Macedonian and Greek army across the Hellespont, Alexander wins his first battle against Achaemenid forces at the Granicus River, opening a decade of conquest that will remake the Greek world.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Charles Le Brun, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Charles Le Brun's 1665 painting Le Passage du Granique, depicting Alexander's forces crossing the Granicus River.

events.title: The Wars of the Diadochi Begin
events.body: Alexander the Great's sudden death without a clear heir plunges his empire into decades of conflict, as his generals carve up his conquests -- including Greece and Macedon -- into rival successor kingdoms.
events.imageAttribution: Map derived from William R. Shepherd's 1911 Historical Atlas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the successor kingdoms carved from Alexander the Great's empire.

events.title: The Colossus of Rhodes Is Completed
events.body: The sculptor Chares of Lindos finishes a bronze statue of the sun god Helios towering over the harbor of Rhodes, funded by the sale of siege equipment abandoned after the island's successful defense against Macedonian siege -- a work later counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Sidney Barclay, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century engraving imagining the Colossus of Rhodes standing over the harbor.

events.title: Eratosthenes Calculates the Earth's Circumference
events.body: Working as chief librarian at Alexandria, Eratosthenes compares the sun's angle at noon in Alexandria and Syene to calculate the Earth's circumference, arriving at a figure remarkably close to the modern measurement.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by cmglee, David Monniaux, and jimht at shaw dot ca, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A diagram illustrating Eratosthenes' method for calculating the Earth's circumference using shadow angles at Alexandria and Syene.

events.title: Rome Conquers Greece
events.body: Roman forces defeat the Achaean League at Corinth and raze the city, ending Greek political independence and absorbing the Greek world into Rome's expanding Mediterranean empire.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Tony Robert-Fleury, photographed by Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting depicting the Roman sack of Corinth in 146 BC.

name: Rome
summary: Rome grew from a legendary founding in 753 BC through a Republic that conquered the Mediterranean, into an Empire under Augustus in 27 BC that split its administration under Diocletian in 293 AD -- the Western half finally collapsing in 476 AD while the Eastern half continued for another millennium as the Byzantine Empire.
imageAttribution: Map by Roke, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map tracing Roman territory from the early Republic through the Empire's height and eventual east-west division.

events.title: Legendary Founding of Rome
events.body: Tradition holds that Romulus founds the city of Rome on the Palatine Hill after being raised by a she-wolf; archaeology instead points to a gradual merger of hilltop villages around the same period.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rabax63, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Capitoline Wolf, a bronze sculpture of a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, Rome's legendary founders.

events.title: The Roman Republic Is Established
events.body: Rome's last king is overthrown and replaced with elected magistrates and a Senate, beginning nearly five centuries of republican government before power concentrates again under the emperors.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ifly6, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Roman Republic territory in 44 BC, near the end of the Republican era.

events.title: Rome Codifies the Twelve Tables
events.body: Plebeian pressure for written law leads to the inscription of the Twelve Tables in the Roman Forum, giving ordinary citizens a public reference for legal rights that had previously been interpreted only by patrician judges.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving, artist unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A period engraving depicting the Twelve Tables, the earliest codification of Roman law.

events.title: Gauls Rout Rome at the Allia
events.body: A Gallic army led by Brennus crushes the Roman legions at the Allia River and marches on to sack the city itself, a catastrophe so severe that Romans later mark the date as one to avoid for any new undertaking.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Gustave Surand, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting imagining the Roman rout at the Battle of the Allia.

events.title: Rome Defeats Hannibal at Zama
events.body: Scipio Africanus decisively defeats Hannibal's Carthaginian army in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War and breaking Carthage as a rival power in the Mediterranean for good.
events.imageAttribution: Sculpture by Sébastien Slodtz, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 18th-century marble sculpture of Hannibal Barca counting the rings taken from Roman knights killed at Cannae.

events.title: Spartacus Leads a Slave Revolt
events.body: Spartacus and a band of fellow gladiators break out of a training school at Capua and rally tens of thousands of enslaved people into an army that defeats several Roman forces before being crushed two years later.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Soerfm, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Denis Foyatier's 1830 marble statue of Spartacus breaking his chains, now in the Louvre.

events.title: Caesar Reforms the Calendar
events.body: Julius Caesar overhauls Rome's chronically manipulated lunar calendar into a 365-day solar year with a leap day every fourth year, a system that keeps the seasons aligned without priestly intervention and remains the basis of the modern calendar.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Ángel M. Felicísimo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern photograph of a bust portraying Julius Caesar.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.body: A group of senators stab Caesar to death in the Theatre of Pompey on the Ides of March, hoping to save the Republic from his growing personal power -- instead triggering the civil wars that end it.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Vincenzo Camuccini, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Vincenzo Camuccini's early 19th-century painting La morte di Cesare (The Death of Caesar), depicting the assassination in the Senate.

events.title: Octavian Defeats Antony and Cleopatra at Actium
events.body: Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa destroys the combined navy of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off the coast of western Greece, leaving Octavian the unchallenged master of the Roman world four years before he takes the name Augustus.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mark Landon, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A carved relief depicting the naval Battle of Actium.

events.title: Augustus Becomes Rome's First Emperor
events.body: Octavian, Caesar's adopted heir, takes the title Augustus after defeating his rivals in the civil wars, ending the Republic in all but name and founding the Roman Empire he will rule for over 40 years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Justin Benttinen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Augustus of Prima Porta, a marble statue of Augustus in military dress and one of the best-known portraits of the emperor.

events.title: The Ara Pacis Is Dedicated
events.body: The Roman Senate consecrates the Ara Pacis Augustae, an altar carved with processions of the imperial family and allegories of peace and abundance, celebrating the stability Augustus has brought after decades of civil war.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rabax63, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The front facade of the Ara Pacis Augustae, Augustus's altar of peace.

events.title: Germanic Tribes Destroy Three Roman Legions
events.body: An alliance of Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushes and annihilates three Roman legions under Varus in a forest north of the Rhine, a defeat so severe that Rome abandons its ambitions to conquer Germania east of the river.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Agnete, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The epitaph of centurion Marcus Caelius, who died in the battle against Arminius's forces.

events.title: The Colosseum Opens
events.body: Emperor Titus inaugurates Rome's great amphitheater with a hundred days of games, giving the Empire its most enduring symbol of public spectacle and engineering ambition.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by FeaturedPics, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Colosseum, Rome's great amphitheater, still standing today.

events.title: Hadrian Rebuilds the Pantheon
events.body: Hadrian replaces Agrippa's fire-damaged temple with a new Pantheon crowned by a vast unreinforced concrete dome and open oculus, an engineering feat that still stands as the largest structure of its kind in the world.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by NikonZ7II, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Pantheon's exterior in Rome.

events.title: Caracalla Grants Citizenship to All Free Subjects
events.body: Emperor Caracalla's edict extends full Roman citizenship to nearly every free inhabitant of the Empire, ending the old distinction between citizens and provincial subjects and reshaping who counts as Roman.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of papyrus, artist unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A fragment of a papyrus copy of Caracalla's Constitutio Antoniniana.

events.title: Diocletian Splits the Empire Into the Tetrarchy
events.body: Facing an empire too vast for one ruler to defend, Diocletian institutes a four-way division of power between two senior and two junior emperors -- an arrangement that foreshadows the later permanent split between East and West.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A late 3rd-century bust of Emperor Diocletian from Nikomedia, modern Izmit, Turkey.

events.title: The Edict of Milan Legalizes Christianity
events.body: Emperors Constantine and Licinius agree at Milan to grant religious toleration throughout the Empire, ending the persecution of Christians and setting Rome on a path toward becoming a Christian state within the century.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Marie-Lan Nguyen, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A colossal 4th-century marble portrait head of Emperor Constantine.

events.title: Goths Crush the Eastern Roman Army at Adrianople
events.body: Gothic rebels led by Fritigern annihilate the Eastern Roman field army and kill Emperor Valens outside Adrianople, a disaster that shatters confidence in Roman arms and opens the door to the barbarian settlements that will eventually break up the Western Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Elias84 and Dipa_1965, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing troop movements at the Battle of Adrianople in 378 AD.

events.title: Alaric's Visigoths Sack Rome
events.body: Alaric and his Visigothic army breach Rome's walls and plunder the city for three days, the first time in nearly eight centuries that Rome itself has fallen to a foreign enemy -- a shock that reverberates across the Empire even though Rome is no longer its capital.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Joseph-Noël Sylvestre, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Joseph-Noël Sylvestre's 19th-century painting depicting the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410.

events.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.body: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the last Western emperor, the teenage Romulus Augustulus, at Ravenna -- the traditional date marking the end of the Western Roman Empire, while the Eastern half endures as Byzantium.
events.imageAttribution: American Numismatic Society, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gold solidus coin minted for Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor.

name: Persia
summary: Persia was ruled by three successive empires: the Achaemenids, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC and toppled by Alexander the Great in 330 BC; the Parthians, who threw off Seleucid rule in 247 BC and famously humbled Rome at Carrhae; and the Sasanians, who revived Persian imperial rule in 224 AD and held it until the Arab conquest of 651 AD.
imageAttribution: Map by Cattette, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Achaemenid Empire's territory around 500 BC, near its greatest extent.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Founds the Achaemenid Empire
events.body: Cyrus II defeats the Median Empire and unites the Medes and Persians under Achaemenid rule, founding what will become the largest empire the ancient world had yet seen.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Surenae, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of a winged figure at Pasargadae, Cyrus the Great's capital.

events.title: Cyrus Conquers Babylon, Frees the Jewish Captives
events.body: Cyrus captures Babylon and issues the Cyrus Cylinder, a declaration recording his restoration of displaced peoples and local temples — including freeing the Jewish captives held there since the Babylonian conquest of Jerusalem.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Prioryman, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Cyrus Cylinder, an inscribed clay cylinder recording Cyrus's decrees after taking Babylon, now in the British Museum.

events.title: Darius I Suppresses Rebellions and Carves the Behistun Inscription
events.body: After seizing the Achaemenid throne amid the chaos following Cambyses II's death, Darius I fights nineteen battles in a single year to crush a wave of rebellions across the empire, then has his victory and the defeated pretender kings carved into a cliff face at Behistun in three languages.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Patrick C (Pentocelo), CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Behistun relief showing Darius I standing over the defeated rebel Gaumata.

events.title: Darius I Commissions the Old Persian Cuneiform Script
events.body: Lacking a Persian writing system of their own, Darius I has scribes devise Old Persian cuneiform, a simplified 34-character script with word dividers, for the empire's monumental inscriptions.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Old Persian cuneiform inscription from the tomb of Darius I.

events.title: Darius I Reorganizes the Empire into Satrapies
events.body: Darius I restructures the Achaemenid Empire into thirty-six satrapies, each governed by a satrap under the watch of royal inspectors and independent financial and military officials, and fixes a standard annual tribute for every province.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Georges Jansoone, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief depicting an Achaemenid satrap from Asia Minor, dated to the end of the 6th century BC.

events.title: Construction Begins at Persepolis
events.body: Darius I begins building a new ceremonial capital in the Persian heartland, whose terraces, columned halls, and reliefs will showcase the empire's reach from Egypt to the Indus Valley.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Alborzagros, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Gate of All Nations at Persepolis, the ceremonial entrance to Darius I's palace complex.

events.title: The Apadana Reliefs Depict Delegations from across the Empire
events.body: Sculptors carve the staircases of the Apadana at Persepolis with processions of tribute-bearing delegations from across the empire, from Lydia to Ethiopia, presenting a visual catalogue of Achaemenid rule.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Adam Jones, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bas-relief of tribute bearers on the Apadana staircase at Persepolis.

events.title: The Ionian Revolt Challenges Persian Rule
events.body: Aristagoras of Miletus incites the Greek cities of Ionia to rise against Persian rule; Persia spends six years reconquering the region, crushing the revolt decisively at the Battle of Lade and resettling Miletus's population.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Eric Gaba and MinisterForBadTimes, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A campaign map of the military operations during the Ionian Revolt.

events.title: The Battle of Thermopylae
events.body: Xerxes' invading army is delayed for three days at a narrow mountain pass by a small Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas, whose stand becomes a lasting symbol of resistance even in defeat.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Jacques-Louis David, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Jacques-Louis David's 1814 painting Leonidas at Thermopylae, held at the Louvre.

events.title: The Achaemenid Empire Falls to Alexander the Great
events.body: Darius III, the last Achaemenid king, is killed by his own satraps while fleeing Alexander the Great's invasion, bringing the two-century-old empire to an end.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (detail of the Alexander Mosaic)
events.imageDescription: The Alexander Mosaic, a Roman floor mosaic from Pompeii depicting Alexander the Great's battle against Darius III, now in Naples.

events.title: The Parthian Empire Is Founded
events.body: Arsaces I leads the Parni tribe in seizing the region of Parthia from the crumbling Seleucid Empire, founding a new Iranian dynasty that will rule for the next 470 years.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ro4444 (edited), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Parthian Empire's extent under Mithridates II.

events.title: The Nisa Helmeted Warrior Blends Hellenistic and Iranian Art
events.body: At the Parthian royal residence of Nisa, sculptors model a monumental clay head of a helmeted warrior whose naturalistic Greek-trained modeling and Hellenistic armor sit alongside the frontal, restrained style that will come to define Parthian art.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bruce Allardice, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Nisa helmeted warrior, a clay head from a monumental statue found at Old Nisa.

events.title: Mithridates II Adopts the Title King of Kings
events.body: Mithridates II reorganizes newly won territories in Mesopotamia and the Caucasus as Parthian vassal states and, from around 109 BC, becomes the first Parthian ruler to regularly claim the title "King of Kings" in the Achaemenid imperial tradition.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Classical Numismatic Group, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Silver coin of Mithridates II of Parthia, minted at Rhages.

events.title: The Battle of Carrhae
events.body: A Roman invasion force under Crassus is lured into open desert and destroyed by Parthian cavalry under the general Surena, in one of Rome's most catastrophic defeats.
events.imageAttribution: Theodore Ayrault Dodge, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1892 illustration of the Battle of Carrhae from a history of Roman warfare.

events.title: Vologases I Preserves the Scattered Avesta Texts
events.body: Vologases I orders his subjects to gather and safeguard the surviving Avestan scriptures and teachings, which had been scattered since Alexander's conquest more than two centuries earlier, laying groundwork for the Avesta's eventual compilation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Classical Numismatic Group, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Tetradrachm of Vologases I of Parthia, minted at Seleucia.

events.title: The Sasanian Dynasty Rises
events.body: Ardashir I defeats the last Parthian king and founds a new Persian empire under the House of Sasan, which will rival Rome and later Byzantium for over four centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ro4444 (edited), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Sasanian Empire's extent under Khosrow II, near its greatest reach.

events.title: Shapur I Captures the Roman Emperor Valerian
events.body: Sasanian king Shapur I defeats a Roman army at Edessa and takes Emperor Valerian prisoner — the first time a reigning Roman emperor is ever captured in battle.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Sasanian rock relief at Naqsh-e Rostam showing Shapur I's triumph over the captured Roman emperor Valerian.

events.title: Shapur I Founds Bishapur, Fusing Persian and Roman Art
events.body: Shapur I founds the city of Bishapur using Roman engineers and craftsmen captured after his victories over Rome, and its palace floors are laid with mosaics of dancers and musicians that blend Sasanian subjects with Roman mosaic technique.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Sasanian-era mosaics from the palace of Shapur I at Bishapur, now in the National Museum of Iran.

events.title: Shapur I Founds the Academy of Gondishapur
events.body: Shapur I builds a new city in Khuzestan populated partly by Roman prisoners taken during his campaigns against Rome, founding an academy there that grows into a leading center for medicine, philosophy, and science, complete with a hospital and library.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Alireza.heydear, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ruins at the site of the ancient city of Gondishapur in Khuzestan, Iran.

events.title: Kartir Lays the Foundations of a Zoroastrian State Church
events.body: Under Bahram I, the high priest Kartir secures state backing for a centralized Zoroastrian priesthood, gains authority over judicial affairs, and claims to have suppressed rival faiths including Christians, Jews, Mandaeans, Manichaeans, and Buddhists across the empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Darafsh Kaviyani, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Naqsh-e Rajab, site of a Sasanian rock relief and inscription associated with the priest Kartir.

events.title: The Sacred Fire of Adur Gushnasp Is Enshrined at Takht-e Soleymān
events.body: Zoroastrian priests establish one of the empire's three most sacred fires, Adur Gushnasp, at a mountaintop shrine in Media; Sasanian kings including Bahram V and Khosrow I make pilgrimages there for coronations, festivals, and blessings before military campaigns.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Salar Arkan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ruins of the fire temple and city at Takht-e Soleymān, site of the Sasanian sacred fire Adur Gushnasp.

events.title: Khosrow I Builds the Grand Arch at Ctesiphon
events.body: Khosrow I raises a vast brick vault at Ctesiphon, the Sasanian capital, as part of a palace complex whose archway becomes the largest free-standing vault built before the modern era, engineered without supporting scaffolding through angled courses of brick.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Safa Daneshvar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The remains of Taq Kasra, the grand arched vault of the Sasanian palace at Ctesiphon.

events.title: Khosrow I Reforms Taxation and the Military
events.body: Khosrow I replaces variable, yield-based taxes with a fixed land-survey tax and a poll tax paid directly into the royal treasury, and reorganizes the army into four regional commands, opening the cavalry to the newly empowered dehqan gentry.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Classical Numismatic Group, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Coin of Khosrow I, minted at Gundeshapur.

events.title: Borzuya Translates the Panchatantra into Pahlavi
events.body: The physician Borzuya translates the Sanskrit fable collection Panchatantra into Pahlavi at the Sasanian court, a text that will later pass into Arabic as Kalila wa-Dimna and carry Indian storytelling across the Islamic world.
events.imageAttribution: Woodcut by an unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A woodcut depicting Borzuya, a Persian physician at the court of Khosrow I.

events.title: Khosrow II Commissions the Grand Reliefs at Taq-e Bostan
events.body: Khosrow II has monumental rock reliefs carved into a cliff at Taq-e Bostan, depicting his investiture by the gods Ahura Mazda and Anahita alongside scenes of the king mounted in full armor and hunting, among the finest surviving examples of Sasanian sculpture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by جواد, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief at Taq-e Bostan depicting the Sasanian king Khosrow II mounted on horseback in full armor.

events.title: The Sasanian Empire Falls to Arab Conquest
events.body: After the Rashidun Caliphate's forces overrun the empire, the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, is murdered while fleeing near Merv, and Persia is absorbed into the expanding Islamic caliphate.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Javierfv1212, edited by HistoryofIran, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Sasanian, Byzantine, and early Muslim territorial borders around the time of the Arab conquest.

name: China
summary: China was unified for the first time by the Qin in 221 BC, and passed through the Han, a long period of division ended by the Sui, the cosmopolitan Tang, and the innovative Song dynasty before the Mongols completed their conquest of the country in 1279 AD.
imageAttribution: Photo by Severin.stalder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling, one of its best-preserved sections.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang Unifies China
events.body: Qin Shi Huang conquers the last rival states and declares himself the first emperor of a unified China, standardizing writing, currency, and law across the new empire.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century portrait of Qin Shi Huang, copied from a 1609 Chinese original.

events.title: Construction Begins on the Great Wall
events.body: Qin Shi Huang orders existing defensive walls linked and extended into a single fortified line across China's northern frontier, the ancestor of the wall that stands today.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Severin.stalder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling, part of the fortifications linked under Qin Shi Huang.

events.title: Liu Bang Founds the Han Dynasty
events.body: After defeating his rival Xiang Yu in the Chu-Han Contention, Liu Bang founds the Han dynasty, which will rule China for four centuries and give the Han Chinese their name.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Ming-dynasty portrait of Liu Bang, posthumously honored as Emperor Gaozu, founder of the Han dynasty.

events.title: Cai Lun Refines Papermaking
events.body: Han court official Cai Lun perfects a process for making paper from bark, hemp, and rags, a cheap and practical writing material that will eventually spread across the world.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Cai Lun, the Han court official credited with refining papermaking.

events.title: The Yellow Turban Rebellion Erupts
events.body: A Daoist-inspired peasant uprising erupts across eastern China in 184, as followers of the Way of Supreme Peace rise against Han rule amid famine and official corruption. The Han court crushes the main revolt within months, but the regional militias raised to suppress it outlast it and fracture imperial authority for good.
events.imageAttribution: Map by SY (Seasonsinthesun), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the extent of the Yellow Turban Rebellion in the Eastern Han dynasty.

events.title: The Battle of Red Cliffs
events.body: An outnumbered alliance of Liu Bei and Sun Quan destroys Cao Cao's fleet on the Yangtze River using fire ships, routing his much larger army. The defeat ends Cao Cao's bid to reunify China under his own rule and sets up the three-way split of the Three Kingdoms period.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by User Jie, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The traditional site of the Battle of Red Cliffs on the Yangtze River, photographed in 2003.

events.title: Cao Pi Ends the Han Dynasty
events.body: Cao Pi forces the last Han emperor, Xian, to abdicate in his favor, formally ending four centuries of Han rule and founding the state of Cao Wei. Rival claimants Liu Bei and Sun Quan soon proclaim their own empires, opening the Three Kingdoms period.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Yan Liben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A detail of Cao Pi from the Thirteen Emperors Scroll, attributed to the Tang-dynasty painter Yan Liben.

events.title: The Jin Dynasty Reunifies China
events.body: Jin forces conquer the southern state of Eastern Wu, ending the Three Kingdoms period and reuniting China under a single ruler for the first time since the Han collapse six decades earlier. The reunification proves short-lived, as succession wars and nomadic invasions fracture the Jin within a generation.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ian Kiu, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Map of the Western Jin dynasty's territory around 280 CE, after its reunification of China.

events.title: The Yungang Grottoes Are Carved
events.body: Northern Wei monks begin carving the Yungang Grottoes into a cliff face near the capital Pingcheng, eventually completing dozens of Buddhist cave shrines filled with monumental stone Buddhas under imperial and private patronage. The site becomes one of the great showcases of early Chinese Buddhist sculpture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Buddhist cave shrines at the Yungang Grottoes near Datong.

events.title: Northern Wei Moves Its Capital and Adopts Han Customs
events.body: Emperor Xiaowen relocates the Northern Wei capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang and orders the ruling Xianbei elite to adopt Han Chinese dress, language, and surnames. The sinicization campaign accelerates the fusion of nomadic and Chinese elites that shapes the reunified empires to follow.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei.

events.title: Sui Wendi Reunifies China
events.body: Emperor Wen ends nearly four centuries of division following the Han collapse, reuniting China under the short-lived Sui dynasty and laying the groundwork for the Grand Canal and the Tang golden age that follows.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Yan Liben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional Chinese portrait of Emperor Wen of Sui, founder of the short-lived Sui dynasty.

events.title: The Grand Canal Is Completed
events.body: Emperor Yang of Sui completes a system of canals linking the Yellow and Yangtze river basins, creating a single waterway that lets grain and goods move between north and south China. The canal becomes the backbone of the empire's economy for the next thousand years, even as the labor demands used to build it help provoke revolt against the Sui.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by EditQ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Wanning Bridge, spanning a section of the Grand Canal.

events.title: The Sui Dynasty Falls
events.body: Years of failed campaigns against Goguryeo and crushing conscription for canal and wall projects trigger rebellions across the empire, and Emperor Yang is assassinated by his own guards at Jiangdu. The Sui collapses after only 37 years, clearing the way for the Tang dynasty.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Yan Liben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A detail of Emperor Yang of Sui from the Thirteen Emperors Scroll, attributed to Yan Liben.

events.title: Tang Taizong Becomes 'Heavenly Khan'
events.body: Emperor Taizong's defeat of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate leads the steppe peoples to acclaim him 'Heavenly Khan,' a title recognizing Tang authority over both China and the nomadic frontier.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of Emperor Taizong of Tang.

events.title: Xuanzang Returns from His Pilgrimage to India
events.body: The monk Xuanzang returns to Chang'an after a seventeen-year overland pilgrimage to India, bringing back hundreds of Buddhist texts to resolve contradictions in the scriptures then circulating in China. His translations and travel account reshape Chinese Buddhism and become a major historical source on Central Asia and India.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional depiction of the monk Xuanzang on his journey to India.

events.title: Wu Zetian Becomes Emperor
events.body: Wu Zetian deposes her own son and proclaims herself huangdi, founding the short-lived Zhou dynasty and becoming the only woman to rule China in her own right rather than as a regent or consort. She governs from Luoyang for fifteen years before being forced to abdicate and restore the Tang.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by wanghongliu, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gilded statue of Wu Zetian at Huangze Temple.

events.title: An Lushan Rebellion Devastates Tang China
events.body: General An Lushan revolts against the Tang court, igniting an eight-year civil war so destructive that census records suggest China's population fell by tens of millions -- a blow the dynasty never fully recovers from.
events.imageAttribution: Map by SY, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the territory affected by the An Lushan Rebellion.

events.title: The Diamond Sutra Is Printed
events.body: A woodblock-printed copy of the Diamond Sutra is produced for free distribution, its colophon dating it precisely to 868. Discovered centuries later at the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, it survives as the world's oldest complete dated printed book.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A page from the 868 CE printed copy of the Diamond Sutra, now in the British Library.

events.title: The Tang Dynasty Falls
events.body: The warlord Zhu Wen forces the last Tang emperor to abdicate, ending nearly 300 years of Tang rule and founding the Later Liang dynasty. His act opens the fractured Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period that lasts until the Song reunification in 960.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of Zhu Wen, Emperor Taizu of Later Liang.

events.title: The Song Dynasty Is Founded
events.body: General Zhao Kuangyin is proclaimed emperor by his own troops and founds the Song dynasty, ushering in an era of economic growth, urbanization, and technological innovation like gunpowder and movable-type printing.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of Song Taizu (Zhao Kuangyin), founder of the Song dynasty, from a scroll later remounted in the Qing dynasty.

events.title: Bi Sheng Invents Movable Type Printing
events.body: The artisan Bi Sheng develops the world's first movable type system, using individually carved and fired clay characters that can be arranged and reused for different texts. Wood and metal type later prove more durable, but his invention anticipates print technology that will not reach Europe for another four centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Popolon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction of Bi Sheng's movable clay type printing tools at the China Printing Museum.

events.title: Wang Anshi Launches the New Policies
events.body: Chancellor Wang Anshi launches a sweeping program of economic and administrative reforms, including state loans to farmers, a reorganized tax system, and a merit-based military draft, aiming to strengthen the Song state's finances and defenses. The New Policies split the court into bitter reformist and conservative factions and are repeatedly overturned and revived for decades after his death.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of the Song-dynasty chancellor Wang Anshi.

events.title: The Jingkang Incident Ends the Northern Song
events.body: Jurchen Jin forces storm the Song capital Bianjing, capturing Emperor Huizong, his son Emperor Qinzong, and thousands of the imperial court. A surviving prince flees south and re-establishes the dynasty as the Southern Song, but the north is lost to the Jin for good.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Emperor Huizong of Song, captured during the Jingkang Incident.

events.title: Mongols Conquer the Song Dynasty
events.body: Kublai Khan's fleet destroys the last Song loyalist forces at the naval Battle of Yamen, completing the Mongol conquest of China and founding the Yuan dynasty.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by 长夜无风, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The modern memorial site at Yamen, Guangdong, marking the naval battle that ended the Song dynasty.

name: Maya
summary: The Maya developed one of the ancient world's most sophisticated civilizations across the tropical lowlands of modern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and Honduras, without ever unifying into a single empire. Preclassic cities like Nakbe and El Mirador pioneered monumental pyramid-building by the first millennium BC; the Classic Period (c. 250-900 AD) saw rival city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, and Copán compete through warfare, dynastic marriage, and monumental art before a still-debated collapse depopulated the southern lowlands; and in the Postclassic era power shifted north to Chichen Itza and then Mayapan, whose fall in the 1440s fragmented the Yucatán into small kingdoms that resisted Spanish conquest until the last one fell in 1697.
imageAttribution: Photo by Raymond Ostertag, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: Temple I, the Great Jaguar pyramid, rising over the Great Plaza at Tikal.

events.title: Monumental Construction Begins at Nakbe
events.body: In the Mirador Basin, Nakbe becomes one of the first Maya settlements to raise large stone platforms and pyramids, marking the start of large-scale Maya monumental architecture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Simon Burchell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A small temple pyramid at Nakbe, one of the earliest major Maya sites.

events.title: El Mirador Rises as the First Great Maya City
events.body: Nearby El Mirador eclipses Nakbe to become the largest Preclassic Maya city, its La Danta pyramid ranking among the largest structures built anywhere in the ancient world by volume.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Konjiki1, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The La Danta pyramid complex at El Mirador, one of the largest structures of the ancient world by volume.

events.title: The San Bartolo Murals Depict Maya Creation Mythology and Kingship
events.body: At San Bartolo in the Petén, muralists paint scenes of the maize god's birth and a king's coronation blessed by the gods -- the oldest known Maya paintings, showing that divine kingship was already established centuries earlier than once thought.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Authenticmaya, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A mural fragment from San Bartolo depicting Preclassic Maya religious art, discovered in 2003.

events.title: Preclassic Maya Cities Collapse
events.body: El Mirador and most other major Preclassic centers are abandoned amid drought and political breakdown, closing out the Preclassic period before power later shifts to cities like Tikal.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Authenticmaya, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The jungle-covered Tigre pyramid at El Mirador, abandoned along with the rest of the city by about 150 AD.

events.title: The Classic Period Begins
events.body: Maya city-states like Tikal and Calakmul enter their peak era of monumental architecture, written history, and dynastic rivalry.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mundo Maya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Plaza at Tikal, one of the dominant Maya city-states of the Classic Period.

events.title: Teotihuacan's Entrada Remakes Tikal
events.body: A Teotihuacan-backed general, Siyaj K'ak', arrives at Tikal the same day its king dies in battle; within a year a new Teotihuacan-aligned dynasty holds the throne and Tikal's power surges as the distant central Mexican city's proxy in the Maya lowlands.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Greg Willis, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Stela 31 at Tikal, which depicts king Siyaj Chan K'awiil II and records the aftermath of the 378 AD entrada.

events.title: K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' Founds the Copán Dynasty
events.body: A warrior-king linked to Tikal and the distant city of Teotihuacan establishes himself as Copán's first ajaw, founding a royal dynasty that will rule the southeastern Maya kingdom for four centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by DuendeThumb, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Classic-period ceramic incense burner from Copán believed to depict K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', founder of the city's ruling dynasty.

events.title: Pakal Ascends the Throne at Palenque
events.body: Twelve-year-old K'inich Janaab' Pakal begins a 68-year reign that will make Palenque one of the Classic Period's greatest artistic centers.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
