events.imageDescription: The jade funerary mask and burial regalia of K'inich Janaab' Pakal, displayed at Mexico City's National Museum of Anthropology.

events.title: Kan Bahlam II Dedicates the Group of the Cross at Palenque
events.body: Palenque's new king completes three temples honoring the Palenque Triad gods, their carved panels tracing his own accession back to the city's creation mythology and cementing his divine right to rule.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Mdcarrasco, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction illustration of the Temple of the Cross Complex, the three temples Kan Bahlam II dedicated to the Palenque Triad gods.

events.title: Quiriguá Captures and Sacrifices Copán's King
events.body: Vassal city Quiriguá defeats its former overlord Copán in battle; king K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat has Copán's ruler Waxaklajuun Ubaah K'awiil beheaded, upending the political order of the southeastern Maya lowlands.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jan Pesula, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Stela E at Quiriguá, a 12-meter monument raised in 771 by K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat, the king who conquered Copán.

events.title: Yajaw Chan Muwaan II Commissions the Bonampak Murals
events.body: Bonampak's ruler has artists cover the walls of a three-room temple with scenes of courtly ceremony, a brutal battle and its aftermath, and bloodletting rites -- commemorating his son Chooj's accession and leaving the most vivid surviving record of Classic Maya court life.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jacob Rus, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: One of the Bonampak murals depicting a battle scene from the reign of Yajaw Chan Muwaan II.

events.title: The Last Long Count Date Is Carved
events.body: Monument 101 at Toniná records the final Classic Maya Long Count inscription, as southern lowland cities are abandoned in the following decades.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by J. Antonio Cruz Coutino, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Templo Mayor pyramid at Toniná, the Chiapas hill-city where Maya scribes carved their last Long Count date in 909.

events.title: Chichen Itza Rises to Dominate the Yucatán
events.body: Chichen Itza grows into the peninsula's dominant power, blending Maya and central Mexican Toltec architectural styles at monuments like El Castillo.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Daniel Schwen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: El Castillo, the step pyramid dedicated to Kukulcan at the center of Chichen Itza.

events.title: Scribes Compile the Dresden Codex
events.body: Maya scribes working in the Chichen Itza region produce the Dresden Codex, a bark-paper book of precise astronomical tables tracking lunar eclipses and the cycle of Venus -- one of only a handful of Maya books to survive the Spanish conquest.
events.imageAttribution: Scan of the Dresden Codex, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Pages of the Dresden Codex showing tables believed to record eclipses and other astronomical cycles.

events.title: Mayapan Becomes the Yucatán's New Capital
events.body: Mayapan, a walled city modeled on Chichen Itza, becomes the political and cultural capital of the Yucatán Maya, eventually growing to more than 4,000 structures.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by SiMeCaIS, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ruins of Mayapan, walled capital of the Yucatán Maya from the 1220s to the 1440s.

events.title: Mayapan Adopts Multepal, a Council of Noble Lineages
events.body: Rather than a single supreme ruler, Mayapan is governed by a council of noble families under the Cocom dynasty's paramount chief, a shared style of rule known as multepal that will hold the fractious city together for two centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by HJPD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A columned hall at Mayapan, seen from the site's Kukulcan pyramid.

events.title: Mayapan Collapses, Fragmenting the Yucatán
events.body: Rebellion topples Mayapan's ruling Cocom dynasty, and the Yucatán Maya splinter into rival, often warring city-states with no single dominant capital.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Pavel Vorobiev, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Panoramic view of Mayapan's ruins from the temple of Kukulcan.

events.title: Nojpetén Falls, Ending Independent Maya Rule
events.body: Spanish forces under Martín de Ursúa storm Nojpetén, the Itza capital on Lake Petén Itzá, ending the last independent Maya kingdom more than 175 years after the conquest of Mexico began.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rafael Amado Deras, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Flores, Guatemala, the modern town built on the island that was once Nojpetén, the Itza Maya capital.

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The Byzantine Empire carried Roman rule forward in the east for over a thousand years after Constantine founded Constantinople in 330 -- surviving Arab sieges, reaching a medieval peak under Basil II, and enduring the Fourth Crusade's sack of its own capital in 1204 -- before finally falling to the Ottomans in 1453.
imageAttribution: Map by Mnohohrishnyi, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire at the end of Justinian I's reign in 565.

events.title: Constantinople Is Founded
events.body: Emperor Constantine dedicates his new capital on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium, a strategically located city that will anchor Roman power in the east for over a thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Cplakidas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A topographical map of Constantinople during the Byzantine period.

events.title: Justinian's Code Is Compiled
events.body: Emperor Justinian I orders the compilation of centuries of Roman law into a single authoritative code, a work that will shape legal systems across Europe for centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th-century manuscript excerpt of the Code of Justinian with medieval legal commentary in the margins.

events.title: The Nika Riots Nearly Topple Justinian
events.body: A week of chariot-racing riots erupts into a full revolt against Justinian I, killing an estimated 30,000 people and burning much of Constantinople -- including the original Hagia Sophia -- before Belisarius crushes the uprising in the Hippodrome.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Dennis G. Jarvis, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Obelisk of Theodosius in Constantinople's Hippodrome, site of the Nika riots' suppression.

events.title: Belisarius Retakes Carthage
events.body: Justinian's general Belisarius destroys the Vandal Kingdom and enters Carthage, restoring Roman rule over North Africa and opening the emperor's campaign to reclaim the lost provinces of the Western Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Cplakidas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Byzantine military operations during the Vandalic War of 533-534.

events.title: The Hagia Sophia Is Completed
events.body: Justinian I dedicates a vast domed cathedral in Constantinople, an architectural triumph that remains the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Adli Wahid, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A photograph of the Hagia Sophia, the great domed cathedral Justinian I built in Constantinople.

events.title: The Plague of Justinian Strikes
events.body: A pandemic later identified with bubonic plague spreads from Egypt into Constantinople, killing as much as two-fifths of the capital's population at its height and crippling the manpower and finances behind Justinian's wars of reconquest.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Jniemenmaa, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Byzantine Empire around 550, near the plague's height, showing Justinian I's reconquests in green.

events.title: The Byzantines Lose Syria at Yarmouk
events.body: Arab forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid rout the Byzantine army over six days of fighting along the Yarmouk River, a defeat that ends Byzantine rule in Syria and opens the Levant to the Rashidun conquest.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from a 14th-century Catalonian manuscript, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A manuscript illustration of the Battle of Yarmouk showing Byzantine and Rashidun forces in combat.

events.title: Alexandria Falls, Ending Roman Egypt
events.body: Arab general Amr ibn al-As enters Alexandria under a negotiated surrender, closing out a three-year campaign that strips the empire of Egypt -- one of its wealthiest provinces and a grain source it had held for nearly 700 years.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Mohammad Adil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Rashidun conquest of Byzantine Egypt in the 7th century.

events.title: Greek Fire Repels the Arab Siege of Constantinople
events.body: A year-long Umayyad siege of the Byzantine capital collapses after Byzantine ships destroy the Arab fleet with Greek fire, an incendiary weapon that burns even on water -- a defeat that halts the Islamic conquests' advance into Europe from the east.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Manasses Chronicle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 14th-century miniature from the Constantine Manasses Chronicle depicting the Arab siege of Constantinople.

events.title: Iconoclasm Divides the Church
events.body: Emperor Leo III orders the removal of a revered image of Christ from the palace's Chalke Gate, opening a decades-long imperial campaign against religious icons that splits the church and populace.
events.imageAttribution: Miniature from the Chludov Psalter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 9th-century manuscript miniature depicting iconoclasts whitewashing an image of Christ.

events.title: The Second Council of Nicaea Restores Icons
events.body: Empress Irene convenes a church council that reverses decades of imperial policy, ruling that venerating icons honors the figures they depict rather than the images themselves and ending the first period of Iconoclasm.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Menologion of Basil II, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 11th-century manuscript depiction of the Second Council of Nicaea.

events.title: Emperor Nikephoros I Is Killed at Pliska
events.body: Bulgar forces under Khan Krum ambush the retreating Byzantine army in a mountain pass, annihilating it and killing Emperor Nikephoros I, whose skull Krum has mounted in silver as a drinking cup.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Manasses Chronicle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A manuscript illustration of Khan Krum's forces attacking the Byzantine army.

events.title: The Rus Convert to Orthodox Christianity
events.body: Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev is baptized at Byzantine Chersonesus and marries the emperor's sister Anna, then brings Orthodox Christianity to his people -- binding the Rus to Byzantine religious and cultural influence for centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Klavdy Lebedev, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A late 19th-century painting depicting the mass baptism of the people of Rus.

events.title: Basil II Crushes Bulgaria at Kleidion
events.body: Byzantine emperor Basil II annihilates the Bulgarian army in a mountain pass, a victory so decisive -- and so brutally followed up -- that it earns him the epithet 'the Bulgar Slayer' and marks the empire's medieval territorial peak.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Manasses Chronicle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A manuscript illustration showing Basil II's victory over the Bulgarians and the death of Tsar Samuel.

events.title: The Great Schism Divides the Church
events.body: Mutual excommunications between the Pope in Rome and the Patriarch of Constantinople formalize a centuries-old rift, splitting Christianity into Catholic and Orthodox branches that remain divided today.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Barrikader, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Christianity's eastern and western allegiances following the 1054 schism.

events.title: The Byzantines Are Routed at Manzikert
events.body: Seljuk forces rout the Byzantine army and capture Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes near Lake Van, a defeat that opens Anatolia -- the empire's core recruiting ground -- to Turkish settlement.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by O. Mustafin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An illustration of the Battle of Manzikert between Byzantine and Seljuk forces.

events.title: Byzantines Recover Nicaea with Crusader Help
events.body: Byzantine forces accompanying the First Crusade negotiate the surrender of Nicaea from its Seljuk garrison, the crusade's first major victory and a rare moment of Byzantine territorial recovery under Alexios I Komnenos.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from a 13th-century French manuscript, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval manuscript illustration of the siege of Nicaea during the First Crusade.

events.title: The Fourth Crusade Sacks Constantinople
events.body: Crusader knights bound for the Holy Land instead storm and pillage Constantinople itself, installing a Latin emperor and shattering Byzantine power so thoroughly that the empire never fully recovers before its final fall two and a half centuries later.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sailko, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: The Byzantines Recapture Constantinople
events.body: Nicaean general Alexios Strategopoulos slips a small force into Constantinople while its Latin garrison is away, ending the Latin Empire and restoring Byzantine rule under Michael VIII Palaiologos after 57 years of exile.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Giuseppe Lorenzo Gatteri and Francesco Zanotto, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century illustration of the Venetian fleet evacuating Latin residents fleeing Constantinople in 1261.

events.title: The Hesychast Controversy Is Resolved
events.body: A Constantinople synod under Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos rules in favor of the monk Gregory Palamas, enshrining his mystical Hesychast theology as Orthodox doctrine after a decade of church dispute.
events.imageAttribution: Icon, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An icon depicting Gregory Palamas, whose theology was upheld at the 1351 synod.

events.title: The Union of Florence Attempts to Reunite the Churches
events.body: Byzantine and Catholic bishops sign an agreement reuniting the Eastern and Western churches in a last bid for Western military aid against the Ottomans -- a union the Constantinople clergy and public reject on the delegation's return, and one that produces no meaningful help before the empire's fall.
events.imageAttribution: Woodcut by Michel Wolgemut and Wilhelm Pleydenwurff, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle woodcut depicting the Council of Florence.

events.title: Constantinople Falls to the Ottomans
events.body: After a 53-day siege using massive cannon to breach the ancient walls, Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and the last continuous link to ancient Rome.
events.imageAttribution: Fresco, Moldovița Monastery, photo by DimiTalen, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern fresco at Moldovița Monastery in Romania depicting the siege of Constantinople.

name: Islamic Caliphates
summary: The Islamic Caliphates passed through three successive dynasties: the Rashidun (632-661), whose rapid conquests carried Islam from Arabia across Persia and North Africa; the Umayyads (661-750), ruling from Damascus at their peak from Spain to India; and the Abbasids (750-1258), whose Baghdad-centered Golden Age ended when the Mongols sacked the city in 1258.
imageAttribution: Map by Mohammad adil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Rashidun Caliphate at its greatest territorial extent.

events.title: The Hijra Marks Year One
events.body: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina to escape persecution, an event so pivotal to the Muslim community that it becomes year one of the Islamic calendar.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Islamic miniature depicting the angel Jibril delivering God's instruction for Muhammad to leave Mecca for Medina.

events.title: The Rashidun Caliphate Begins
events.body: Following Muhammad's death, Abu Bakr is chosen as the first caliph, beginning three decades of rapid conquest that will carry Islamic rule from Arabia across Persia, the Levant, and North Africa.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Mohammad adil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Rashidun Caliphate's territory at its height, following the conquests begun under Abu Bakr.

events.title: The Rashidun Army Shatters Byzantine Power at Yarmouk
events.body: A Rashidun army under Khalid ibn al-Walid destroys a much larger Byzantine force near the Yarmouk River, ending Byzantine rule in Syria and opening the entire Levant to Islamic conquest within a few years.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by an anonymous Catalonian illustrator, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 14th-century manuscript illustration of the Battle of Yarmouk, showing Muslim forces facing Byzantine troops.

events.title: Qadisiyyah Breaks Sasanian Power in Iraq
events.body: Rashidun forces under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas defeat the main Sasanian army near Qadisiyyah, a victory that opens Mesopotamia to Muslim rule and leads to the fall of the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon within months.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from a Shahnameh manuscript, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Persian manuscript illustration of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas's forces defeating the Sasanian general Rostam Farrokhzad.

events.title: The First Fitna Splits the Muslim Community
events.body: The murder of Caliph Uthman triggers five years of civil war among Muhammad's early followers, pitting Ali against the Syrian governor Muawiyah and ending only with Ali's assassination -- a rupture that hardens into the lasting Sunni-Shia divide.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Al Ameer son, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing territory controlled by Caliph Ali and by the governor Muawiyah during the First Fitna.

events.title: Muawiyah I Founds the Umayyad Caliphate
events.body: After a civil war among Muhammad's early followers, Muawiyah I establishes the Umayyad Caliphate from his power base in Damascus, shifting the seat of Islamic rule from Arabia to Syria and founding a dynasty that will expand from Spain to India.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Arab-Sasanian silver coin of Caliph Muawiyah I, minted in the Umayyad Caliphate's early style.

events.title: Husayn Is Killed at Karbala
events.body: Umayyad forces under Caliph Yazid I kill Husayn ibn Ali, the Prophet Muhammad's grandson, and most of his small band at Karbala, an act of martyrdom that becomes the defining trauma of Shia Islam and is commemorated annually on Ashura.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Abbas Al-Musavi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Qajar-era painting depicting the Battle of Karbala.

events.title: The Dome of the Rock Is Completed in Jerusalem
events.body: Caliph Abd al-Malik completes the Dome of the Rock atop Jerusalem's Temple Mount, an octagonal shrine whose gold dome and Quranic inscriptions announce Islam's presence among the older faiths of the holy city.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Ludvig14, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem.

events.title: Abd al-Malik Reforms Coinage and Administration
events.body: Caliph Abd al-Malik replaces Byzantine- and Sasanian-style coins with a new Islamic currency bearing Quranic inscriptions instead of images, and begins converting the caliphate's Greek- and Persian-language bureaucracy to Arabic -- steps that forge a distinct Islamic state identity across the empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An early Umayyad gold dinar of Caliph Abd al-Malik, minted before the later aniconic redesign.

events.title: The Battle of Tours Halts Umayyad Expansion
events.body: A Frankish army under Charles Martel defeats an Umayyad raiding force deep in what is now France, a battle later mythologized as the moment that stopped the Islamic conquests' advance into Western Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Charles de Steuben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours.

events.title: The Abbasid Caliphate Is Founded
events.body: Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah overthrows the Umayyad dynasty and founds the Abbasid Caliphate, which will soon move its capital to the newly built city of Baghdad and preside over an era of scientific and cultural flourishing.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from a Tarikhnama manuscript, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A folio from a Tarikhnama (history) by Balami depicting the proclamation of Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah as the first Abbasid caliph.

events.title: Abd al-Rahman I Founds the Emirate of Córdoba
events.body: The last surviving Umayyad prince, having fled the Abbasid massacre of his family in Damascus, defeats the governor of al-Andalus and establishes an independent emirate at Córdoba -- preserving Umayyad rule in Spain for centuries after the dynasty's fall in the east.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Numismática Pliego, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A silver dirham minted under Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Emirate of Córdoba.

events.title: Al-Khwarizmi Writes the Book That Names Algebra
events.body: Working at Baghdad's House of Wisdom, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi completes Al-Jabr, a treatise systematizing the solution of linear and quadratic equations that later gives algebra its name and becomes Europe's standard mathematics textbook for centuries after its Latin translation.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A page from a manuscript copy of al-Khwarizmi's Al-Jabr.

events.title: The House of Wisdom Flourishes in Baghdad
events.body: Scholars in Baghdad translate and expand upon Greek, Persian, and Indian texts at a great library and translation center, driving advances in mathematics, astronomy, and medicine during the Islamic Golden Age.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Maqamat al-Hariri manuscript (13th century), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A manuscript illustration of a library, from the Maqamat of al-Hariri.

events.title: The Zanj Rebellion Convulses Southern Iraq
events.body: Enslaved and freed Africans led by Ali ibn Muhammad rise up near Basra, building fortresses and a navy that hold off Abbasid armies for fourteen years -- a revolt so costly that it lets provincial strongmen in Egypt and the east break away while the caliphate is consumed fighting it.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ro4444, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Abbasid Caliphate showing the region affected by the Zanj Rebellion.

events.title: The Fatimid Caliphate Is Founded in North Africa
events.body: Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah proclaims himself caliph at Raqqada in Ifriqiya, founding a rival Isma'ili Shia caliphate that rejects Abbasid authority and will go on to rule an empire stretching from North Africa to Egypt and the Hejaz.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Omar-toons, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Fatimid Caliphate's territory over the course of its history.

events.title: Abd al-Rahman III Proclaims Himself Caliph
events.body: Facing a challenge to Sunni legitimacy from the rival Fatimid caliphs in North Africa, the emir of Córdoba Abd al-Rahman III declares himself caliph, elevating his state into the Caliphate of Córdoba and asserting religious authority equal to Baghdad's.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Numismática Pliego, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A silver dirham minted under Abd al-Rahman III, the first Caliph of Córdoba.

events.title: The Buyids Take Control of Baghdad
events.body: The Daylamite warlord Ahmad ibn Buya conquers Baghdad and takes the title Mu'izz al-Dawla, reducing the Abbasid caliph to a powerless figurehead under Shia Buyid military rule for the next century.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ro4444, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the three Buyid emirates around 970.

events.title: The Fatimids Found Cairo and al-Azhar
events.body: After conquering Egypt, Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli lays out a new fortified capital, al-Qahira (Cairo), and founds the mosque of al-Azhar beside it -- soon to grow into one of the Islamic world's foremost centers of learning.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Wildoo78, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Al-Azhar Mosque in Cairo.

events.title: The Caliphate of Córdoba Dissolves Into Taifa Kingdoms
events.body: Two decades of civil war following the death of the military strongman al-Mansur splinter the Caliphate of Córdoba into dozens of competing Taifa kingdoms, ending unified Umayyad rule in al-Andalus for good.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Falconaumanni, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Taifa kingdoms that emerged from the Caliphate of Córdoba's collapse.

events.title: Seljuk Turks Take Control of Baghdad
events.body: Sultan Tughril leads Seljuk forces into Baghdad and ends Shia Buyid domination of the Abbasid court, reducing the caliph to a religious figurehead under Sunni Turkic military rule for the remainder of the caliphate's existence.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A miniature depicting the Seljuk sultan Tughril Beg enthroned in Nishapur.

events.title: Saladin Ends Fatimid Rule in Egypt
events.body: Saladin abolishes the Fatimid Caliphate on the death of its last caliph and restores nominal Abbasid authority over Egypt, founding the Ayyubid dynasty and closing out the two-century-old Shia caliphate centered on Cairo.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Classical Numismatic Group, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A silver dirham of Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty.

events.title: The Mongols Sack Baghdad
events.body: Hulagu Khan's Mongol army razes Baghdad and executes the last Abbasid caliph, destroying the city's libraries and irrigation works in a catastrophe that ends the Abbasid Caliphate and is remembered as a turning point in the Islamic world's fortunes.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval illustration of the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

name: Khmer Empire
summary: Founded in 802 when Jayavarman II is consecrated as a universal monarch on Phnom Kulen, the Khmer Empire grows into the dominant power of mainland Southeast Asia, centered on the temple-city of Angkor. Its kings build an unmatched sequence of monuments and hydraulic works, from Indravarman I's first sandstone temple-mountain to Angkor Wat under Suryavarman II and the fortified capital of Angkor Thom under Jayavarman VII, who rebuilds the empire after a Cham fleet sacks the capital in 1177 and endows it with hospitals and highways. The state religion swings between Hinduism and Buddhism more than once, settling permanently on Theravada Buddhism by the end of the 13th century, even as a Chinese envoy's eyewitness account of Angkor survives as one of the empire's only outside records. Repeated wars with the rising Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya erode Khmer power over the empire's final century until Angkor itself is captured and abandoned in 1431.
imageAttribution: Map by Jembezmamy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of Southeast Asia circa 900 CE, showing the Khmer Empire's territory alongside neighboring Champa and other states.

events.title: Jayavarman II Founds the Khmer Empire
events.body: Atop Mount Mahendraparvata, brahmin priests consecrate Jayavarman II as a chakravartin, or universal monarch, establishing the devaraja cult of divine kingship and unifying rival principalities into the new Khmer Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Xufanc, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Phnom Kulen, the mountain range known in antiquity as Mahendraparvata, where Jayavarman II was consecrated as universal monarch.

events.title: Indravarman I Builds Bakong and a New Reservoir
events.body: At his capital of Hariharalaya, Indravarman I dedicates Bakong, the first Khmer temple-mountain built entirely of sandstone, and completes the Indratataka, a reservoir over three kilometers long that establishes the water-management system that will sustain Angkor for centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Photo Dharma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Bakong, the sandstone temple-mountain Indravarman I built as his state temple at Hariharalaya.

events.title: Yasodharapura Becomes the Capital
events.body: King Yasovarman I moves his court to a new capital, Yasodharapura, anchored by the temple-mountain of Phnom Bakheng, dedicated to Shiva on a hill overlooking the site that becomes Angkor.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Satdeep Gill, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Phnom Bakheng, the Shiva temple-mountain at the center of Yasovarman I's new capital, Yasodharapura.

events.title: Yasovarman I Completes the East Baray
events.body: King Yasovarman I finishes the East Baray, an artificial reservoir more than seven kilometers long holding over 36 million cubic meters of water, part of the hydraulic network that comes to define the city of Angkor.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The East Mebon temple, built on what was once an island at the center of the East Baray reservoir.

events.title: Courtiers Consecrate Banteay Srei
events.body: Royal counsellors Yajnavaraha and Vishnukumara dedicate Banteay Srei, a Hindu temple whose pink sandstone reliefs are carved with a delicacy closer to goldsmithing than stonework, making it one of the empire's finest artistic achievements even though no king ever commissioned it.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of a Banteay Srei bas relief, public domain, via Wikipedia
events.imageDescription: A carved sandstone relief at Banteay Srei, showing the temple's intricate ornamental style.

events.title: Suryavarman I Ends a Civil War and Reforms the Bureaucracy
events.body: After nearly a decade of war against rival claimant Jayavirahvarman, Suryavarman I secures undisputed control of Angkor and summons some 4,000 local officials to the royal palace to swear a personal oath of allegiance, binding the empire's administration directly to the throne.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Phimeanakas, the royal palace temple at Angkor associated with Suryavarman I's era.

events.title: Construction of Angkor Wat Begins
events.body: Suryavarman II commissions the largest religious monument in the world as his state temple, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Angkor Wat, the front of the main temple complex, photographed in the late afternoon.

events.title: The Cham Sack Angkor
events.body: A Cham fleet under Jaya Indravarman IV sails up the Tonlé Sap, sacks the Khmer capital of Yasodharapura, and kills King Tribhuvanadityavarman, beginning a four-year occupation of the Khmer heartland.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Photo Dharma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bas-relief at the Bayon temple depicting the Khmer-Cham naval battles fought on the Tonlé Sap.

events.title: Jayavarman VII Expels the Cham and Rebuilds Angkor
events.body: After a four-year campaign to drive out the Cham occupiers, Jayavarman VII is crowned king and launches the empire's largest building program, founding the walled capital of Angkor Thom around the Bayon, his state temple.
events.imageAttribution: Sculpture photographed by Suzan Black, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A sandstone head presumed to depict King Jayavarman VII, in the Bayon style, now in the Musée Guimet, Paris.

events.title: Jayavarman VII Builds a Network of Hospitals
events.body: As part of his reconstruction of the empire, Jayavarman VII endows 102 hospital chapels across the kingdom, among them Ta Prohm Kel near Angkor Thom, alongside a network of roads lined with rest houses every fifteen kilometers for travelers.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Arabsalam, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ta Prohm Kel, one of the 102 hospital chapels built across the empire under Jayavarman VII.

events.title: Jayavarman VIII Reverses Course to Hinduism
events.body: Breaking with three generations of royal Buddhist patronage, King Jayavarman VIII restores Shaivite Hinduism as the state religion, ordering Buddha images defaced or removed from temples across the empire, including the central Buddha at the Bayon, which is cast into a well.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Dmitry A. Mottl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Bayon at Angkor Thom, where Jayavarman VIII's iconoclasm reportedly cast the temple's central Buddha image into a well.

events.title: Jayavarman VIII Buys Peace With the Mongol Yuan Court
events.body: As Kublai Khan's Yuan fleet campaigns against neighboring Champa, Jayavarman VIII avoids the same fate by submitting Khmer tribute to the Mongol court, a relationship of gifts and missions that continues for years afterward and keeps the empire outside the Yuan conquests reshaping mainland Southeast Asia.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Araniko, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A court portrait of Kublai Khan, the Yuan emperor whose fleet campaigned through mainland Southeast Asia in the 1280s.

events.title: Indravarman III Makes Theravada Buddhism the State Religion
events.body: Indravarman III deposes his father-in-law Jayavarman VIII and takes the throne as a devout follower of Theravada Buddhism, which he establishes as the state religion, a change that endures long after the empire itself collapses.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Cerie1914, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Buddhist statue of the bodhisattva Lokesvara from Preah Khan temple at Angkor.

events.title: A Chinese Envoy Records Daily Life
events.body: Zhou Daguan, an envoy of the Yuan dynasty, spends nearly a year at Angkor and later writes The Customs of Cambodia, the only detailed eyewitness account of the empire that survives.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Photo Dharma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bas-relief at the Bayon depicting a scene of everyday Khmer domestic life, of the kind Zhou Daguan described in his account.

events.title: Ayutthaya Captures Angkor for the First Time
events.body: After a siege of nearly a year and a half, King Uthong's Siamese army from the newly founded Ayutthaya Kingdom captures Angkor, installs his son as a puppet ruler over the Khmer, and carries prisoners and treasure back to the new Siamese capital.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Colin W, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The south gate of Angkor Thom, the fortified capital that Ayutthaya's army besieged and captured in 1353.

events.title: Khmer Forces Retake Angkor From Siamese Rule
events.body: After years in exile, Prince Suryavamsa Rajadhiraja leads an army back to Angkor, drives out the Siamese garrison installed after the 1353 capture, and reclaims the throne, though the reprieve from Ayutthayan pressure proves temporary.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Stephen Bain, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The east gate of Angkor Thom, known as the Gate of the Dead.

events.title: Ayutthaya Captures Angkor a Second Time
events.body: Following the death of the Khmer king, Siamese King Ramesuan besieges and captures Angkor once more, installs a vassal ruler, and deports tens of thousands of Khmer captives to Ayutthaya, a blow the empire never fully recovers from before its final fall in 1431.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sabyk2001, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Wat Phra Si Sanphet in Ayutthaya, the Siamese capital whose kings twice captured Angkor in the empire's final century.

events.title: Ayutthaya Sacks Angkor
events.body: A Siamese army from Ayutthaya captures and loots the Khmer capital after a prolonged siege, prompting King Ponhea Yat to relocate the royal court south toward present-day Phnom Penh.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Supanut Arunoprayote, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ta Prohm, one of the Angkor temples later reclaimed by jungle after the capital's abandonment.

name: Mongol Empire
summary: Founded in 1206 when a kurultai of steppe chieftains proclaims Temüjin as Genghis Khan, the Mongol Empire grows within two generations into the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled, stretching from the Sea of Japan to the edge of Central Europe. Mongol armies topple the Khwarazmian Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate, while cavalry under Batu Khan and Subutai push as far west as Hungary and Poland before a Mamluk army halts their advance at Ain Jalut. Beyond conquest, the empire hosts a formal debate between Christian, Buddhist, and Muslim envoys at its capital, Karakorum, and Kublai Khan raises a legendary summer palace at Shangdu (Xanadu), before a war of succession after Möngke Khan's death splits the realm into four largely independent khanates by the 1260s; the largest, Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty, rules China until Ming rebels drive the Mongols back to the steppe in 1368.
imageAttribution: Map by Wengier (derivative of a map by Teaandcrumpets), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of Asia's political boundaries in 1335, near the Mongol Empire's territorial peak.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongol Tribes
events.body: A kurultai of steppe chieftains gathers at the source of the Onon River and proclaims Temüjin as Genghis Khan, "universal ruler," ending decades of tribal warfare and setting off the fastest territorial expansion in history.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by unknown artist, digitized by the National Palace Museum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A posthumous portrait of Genghis Khan (Taizu), from the Yuan imperial portrait album.

events.title: The Invasion of Khwarazm Begins
events.body: After the governor of Otrar seizes a Mongol trade caravan and executes its merchants, Genghis Khan turns west and invades the Khwarazmian Empire, destroying its great Central Asian cities within two years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Coopypasted, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An aerial view of the ruins of Otrar, whose governor's seizure of a Mongol caravan triggered the invasion of Khwarazm.

events.title: Mongol Cavalry Crush Hungary at Mohi
events.body: Batu Khan and Subutai's twin invasion of Europe culminates on the Sajó River, where a Mongol army annihilates the royal army of King Béla IV, opening the Hungarian plain to two years of occupation before the Mongols unexpectedly withdraw.
events.imageAttribution: Illumination from the Chronicon Pictum (Cod. 2623), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval illustration from Hayton of Corycus's La Flor des estoires, depicting the Battle of Mohi in 1241.

events.title: Möngke Khan Hosts a Debate Between Faiths at Karakorum
events.body: At his court in Karakorum, Möngke Khan stages a formal debate between Christian, Buddhist, and Muslim representatives, each judged by a delegate from their own faith. Franciscan friar William of Rubruck, an envoy from French king Louis IX, takes part and later records the proceedings.
events.imageAttribution: Painting attributed to the atelier of Abdullah Sultan, Shiraz, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Portrait of Möngke Khan, the fourth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.

events.title: Kublai Raises the Summer Capital at Shangdu
events.body: Architect Liu Bingzhong completes Shangdu, later immortalized in the West as Xanadu, blending Mongolian steppe tradition with Chinese urban planning. Kublai Khan formally makes it his summer capital in 1264, splitting his court between it and Dadu each year.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Flaumfeder, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of Shangdu, the former summer capital of the Yuan dynasty.

events.title: The Mongols Sack Baghdad
events.body: Hulagu Khan's army breaches Baghdad's walls, executes the caliph al-Musta'sim, and topples the five-century-old Abbasid Caliphate, extending Mongol power into the heart of the Islamic world.
events.imageAttribution: Painting from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-tawarikh, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval illustration of the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

events.title: Mamluks Halt the Mongols at Ain Jalut
events.body: A Mamluk army from Egypt defeats Hulagu's rearguard near the spring of Ain Jalut in Galilee, the first open-field defeat of a Mongol army and the effective limit of the empire's expansion into the Middle East.
events.imageAttribution: Map by MapMaster, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the campaign leading to the 1260 Battle of Ain Jalut.

events.title: The Toluid Civil War Splits the Empire
events.body: Kublai Khan's younger brother Ariq Böke surrenders after a four-year war of succession, but the fighting has already broken the unified Mongol Empire into four largely independent khanates: the Yuan, the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, and the Ilkhanate.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Miskin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1596 illustration from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tavarikh depicting Ariq Böke's defeat by Kublai Khan's forces.

events.title: Kublai Khan Founds the Yuan Dynasty
events.body: Genghis Khan's grandson declares a new Chinese dynasty from his capital at Dadu, ruling simultaneously as Great Khan of the Mongols and emperor of China.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by Araniko, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A posthumous portrait of Kublai Khan, painted to make him appear younger than his actual age.

events.title: Ghazan Converts the Ilkhanate to Islam
events.body: On seizing power in the Ilkhanate, Ghazan publicly converts from Buddhism to Islam, and much of the Mongol military elite in Iran and Iraq follows him. The conversion permanently realigns the westernmost khanate, cementing Islam as the dominant faith of Mongol-ruled Iran.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by an unknown Mongol artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ghazan and his wife pictured at court in a late-13th-century Mongol manuscript.

events.title: The Yuan Dynasty Falls
events.body: Ming rebels led by Zhu Yuanzhang capture the Yuan capital at Dadu, driving the Mongols back to the steppe and ending nearly a century of Mongol rule over China.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait of the Hongwu Emperor (Zhu Yuanzhang), digitized by the National Palace Museum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A seated portrait of Emperor Ming Taizu (Zhu Yuanzhang), who founded the Ming dynasty after the Yuan's fall.

name: Mali Empire
summary: The Mali Empire rises from the Mandinka heartland along the upper Niger River, founded by Sundiata Keita after his victory at Kirina in 1235. Under Mansa Musa, its ninth ruler, the empire reaches its greatest wealth and territorial extent, and his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca makes Mali's gold famous across the Islamic world. Timbuktu flourishes as a hub of trade and Islamic scholarship under Mali's patronage, but a long, uneven decline follows Mansa Musa's death: a ruinous civil war and treasury mismanagement under Mari Djata II give way to the loss of Timbuktu to Tuareg raiders in 1433 and to rival Songhai in 1468, and after a catastrophic defeat at Djenné in 1599, the empire fragments for good with the death of its last emperor, Mahmud Keita IV, around 1610.
imageAttribution: Map by HetmanTheResearcher, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map showing the territorial extent of the Mali Empire near its height.

events.title: Sundiata Keita Founds the Mali Empire
events.body: Sundiata Keita leads the united Mandinka clans to victory over the Sosso king Sumanguru Kanté at the Battle of Kirina, is crowned Mansa, and builds the conquered Sosso territories into the new Mali Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Franko Khoury, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th- to 15th-century terracotta equestrian figure from Mali, now in the National Museum of African Art.

events.title: Sakura Seizes the Throne and Expands Mali
events.body: Sakura, a former palace dependent from outside the ruling Keita line, seizes power and pushes Mali's borders west to the Atlantic coast and east toward Gao before being killed returning from his own pilgrimage to Mecca around 1300, after which the Keita dynasty is restored.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Franko Khoury, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th- to 15th-century terracotta archer figure from Mali.

events.title: Mansa Musa's Pilgrimage to Mecca
events.body: Mali's emperor travels to Mecca with a caravan reportedly carrying tons of gold, spending so freely in Cairo along the way that he depresses the region's gold prices for years afterward.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration attributed to Abraham Cresques, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Mansa Musa enthroned and holding a gold coin, from the 1375 Catalan Atlas.

events.title: Djinguereber Mosque Built in Timbuktu
events.body: Fresh from his pilgrimage, Mansa Musa commissions the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, part of a wave of building and scholarship that establishes the city as a center of Islamic learning under Mali's patronage.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by KaTeznik, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The courtyard of the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu.

events.title: Ibn Battuta Visits Mali and Documents Suleyman's Rule
events.body: The Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta arrives at Mansa Suleyman's court and later writes the first detailed outside account of the empire, praising the security of its roads even as he judges Suleyman himself far less generous than his predecessor Mansa Musa.
events.imageAttribution: Map, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A historical map showing the territory of the Mali Empire.

events.title: Mari Djata II Wins a Civil War and Squanders the Treasury
events.body: Mari Djata II fights his way to the throne after a short, contested reign by his predecessor Qanba collapses into civil war, then spends the next fourteen years as a wasteful ruler who at one point sells off a twenty-qintar boulder of state gold for a fraction of its worth — a reign the historian Ibn Khaldun later marks as the start of Mali's decline.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Gabriel Moss, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Mali Empire's territory at the end of Mansa Musa's reign, around 1337.

events.title: Tuareg Forces Seize Timbuktu from Mali
events.body: Tuareg raiders led by Akil Ag-Amalwal capture Timbuktu and the nearby trading town of Oualata, stripping Mali of its most famous city decades before Songhai's own conquest of the region.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Anne and David, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A mosque in Timbuktu, the city Mali lost to Tuareg raiders in 1433.

events.title: Songhai Captures Timbuktu
events.body: Sunni Ali's Songhai forces take Timbuktu, which Mali had already lost to Tuareg raiders decades earlier — a milestone in Mali's terminal decline as Songhai rises to become the region's dominant power.
events.imageAttribution: Map by HetmanTheResearcher, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the territorial extent of the Songhai Empire.

events.title: Mansa Mahmud Keita II Opens Relations with Portugal
events.body: Seeking allies against mounting external threats, Mahmud Keita II receives Portuguese envoys Pêro d'Évora and Gonçalo Enes at the Malian court; a follow-up appeal in 1493 for an alliance against the warlord Tenguella comes to nothing.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from Martin Behaim's Erdapfel (1492), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A European depiction of a ruler of Mali, from Martin Behaim's 1492 globe.

events.title: Mali's Defeat at the Battle of Djenné
events.body: Seeking to exploit Songhai's collapse after Morocco's 1591 invasion, Mansa Mahmud Keita IV attacks the trade hub of Djenné but is routed by Moroccan musketeers stationed there, a defeat that shatters what remains of Mali's imperial prestige.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Ondřej Havelka, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Mosque of Djenné, in the city where the 1599 battle was fought.

events.title: Mali Empire Ends with the Death of Mahmud Keita IV
events.body: Mali's last reigning emperor, Mahmud Keita IV, dies after retreating to the fortress of Sorokuru; his three sons divide what remains of the realm among themselves, and no single Keita ruler ever governs a unified Mali again.
events.imageAttribution: Diagram by Jansen.2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A family tree of the Keita dynasty that ruled the Mali Empire.

name: Aztec (Mexica)
summary: Founded in 1325 when the wandering Mexica people build their capital, Tenochtitlan, on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, the Aztec civilization becomes an empire in 1428 when Tenochtitlan joins Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance after defeating the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco. Over the following century Mexica armies and tribute demands extend the alliance's reach across central Mexico, funding a religious capital whose Great Temple is consecrated in 1487 under the ruler Ahuitzotl. Hernán Cortés lands on the Gulf coast in 1519 and, allying with rivals of the Aztecs, marches on Tenochtitlan; after his men are driven out on La Noche Triste in 1520 he returns with a larger force and, aided by a smallpox epidemic that has already killed thousands, besieges and captures the city in 1521, ending Mexica rule.
imageAttribution: Map by Aldan-2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Aztec Empire's extent in 1519, during the reign of Moctezuma II.

events.title: Tenochtitlan Is Founded
events.body: According to legend, the Mexica see an eagle devouring a serpent atop a cactus — the sign their priests had foretold — and found their capital, Tenochtitlan, on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Roberto Cueva del Río, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 20th-century mural, Fundación de Tenochtitlan, by Roberto Cueva del Río, depicting the city's legendary founding.

events.title: The Triple Alliance Forms
events.body: After the Tepanec usurper Maxtla besieges Tenochtitlan and drives the Acolhua ruler Nezahualcoyotl into exile, the Mexica join Texcoco and the breakaway city of Tlacopan to crush Azcapotzalco, forming the Triple Alliance that becomes the Aztec Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Aztec glyphs for the Triple Alliance's member states by XcepticZP and Goldenbrook, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Aztec glyphs representing the three Triple Alliance city-states: Texcoco, Tenochtitlan, and Tlacopan.

events.title: Nezahualcoyotl Is Restored to the Throne of Texcoco
events.body: With military backing from Tenochtitlan's Itzcoatl, the exiled Acolhua prince Nezahualcoyotl retakes Texcoco's throne after the fall of the Tepanecs, beginning a reign in which he becomes the Triple Alliance's most celebrated lawgiver and poet.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Codex Ixtlilxochitl, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A folio from the 16th-century Codex Ixtlilxochitl depicting Nezahualcoyotl, tlatoani of Texcoco.

events.title: A Flood Destroys Tenochtitlan's Aqueduct
events.body: Torrential rains destroy the wooden aqueduct carrying fresh water from the Chapultepec springs, cutting off Tenochtitlan's supply for weeks; Texcoco's king Nezahualcoyotl responds by engineering a sturdier stone-and-mortar replacement along the same route.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diana du Vent, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Surviving arches of the Chapultepec aqueduct, rebuilt along the same route in the colonial era after the original Aztec structures were lost.

events.title: The Flower Wars Begin
events.body: In the wake of a catastrophic four-year drought and famine, priests declare that the gods demand more captives for sacrifice, and the Triple Alliance institutes the xochiyaoyotl — ritualized "flower wars" against Tlaxcala, Huejotzingo, and Cholula that continue for decades.
events.imageAttribution: Collage by Mabarlabin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Imagery representing the flower wars fought between the Aztecs, Tlaxcalans, and neighboring city-states.

events.title: Axayacatl Conquers Tlatelolco
events.body: Tenochtitlan's tlatoani Axayacatl defeats Moquihuix, ruler of the rival twin city Tlatelolco, in battle and subjects it to Tenochtitlan, bringing the entire island and its great marketplace under unified Mexica rule.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration of Moquihuix from the Codex Mendoza, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Moquihuix, the defeated ruler of Tlatelolco, from the Codex Mendoza.

events.title: Axayacatl Is Defeated by the Tarascans
events.body: Pushing west into Michoacán, Tenochtitlan's armies under Axayacatl are routed by the Tarascan (Purépecha) state — the first major Aztec military defeat, and one that permanently checks the empire's westward expansion.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration of Axayacatl from the Codex Azcatitlan, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Axayacatl, sixth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, from the Codex Azcatitlan.

events.title: The Great Temple Is Dedicated
events.body: Ruler Ahuitzotl consecrates the rebuilt Templo Mayor on the final day of the month of Panquetzaliztli, its twin shrines to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc marking the Mexica capital near the height of its power.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by GAED, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A photograph of the excavated ruins of the Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan's Great Temple.

events.title: Moctezuma II Becomes Tlatoani
events.body: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin is crowned as the ninth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, inheriting an empire near its greatest extent that he will rule for nearly two decades before the Spanish arrive.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Codex Durán, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Moctezuma II receiving his crown during his 1502 coronation, illustrated in the 16th-century Codex Durán.

events.title: The New Fire Ceremony Renews the Aztec World
events.body: As the 52-year calendar cycle ends, Moctezuma II leads priests in procession to the hill of Huixachtlan, where a captive is sacrificed and a new flame kindled on his chest as the "fire drill" constellation rises — a ritual the Aztecs believe keeps the sun returning each day.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by AlejandroLinaresGarcia, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A carved stone marking the "new fire" that begins a 52-year cycle on the Aztec calendar, inscribed with the dates One Rabbit and Two Reed.

events.title: Cortés Arrives on the Coast
events.body: Hernán Cortés lands on the Gulf coast and founds Veracruz, then marches inland, defeating and then allying with the Tlaxcalans as he advances toward Tenochtitlan.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by unknown artist (Museo de América collection), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An anonymous portrait of Hernán Cortés, based on a likeness he sent to Paolo Giovio.

events.title: The Spanish Are Driven Out on La Noche Triste
events.body: After Moctezuma II is killed in rioting and Cortés's men loot the palace treasury, the Mexica attack the retreating Spanish column on the causeway out of the city, inflicting heavy losses in what the Spanish call La Noche Triste, the Night of Sorrows.
events.imageAttribution: Anonymous 17th-century painting, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century oil painting depicting the Spanish retreat from Tenochtitlan under Mexica attack, known as La Noche Triste.

events.title: Cuitláhuac's Brief Reign Ends in Epidemic
events.body: Elected tlatoani after the Spanish are driven from the city, Cuitláhuac organizes Tenochtitlan's defense for just 80 days before dying, likely of the smallpox epidemic sweeping the valley, and is succeeded by his nephew Cuauhtémoc.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration of Cuitláhuac from Bernardino de Sahagún's Primeros Memoriales, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Cuitláhuac, the tenth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, from the 16th-century Primeros Memoriales.

events.title: The Fall of Tenochtitlan
events.body: After a three-month siege and a smallpox epidemic that has already killed thousands, including the previous emperor Cuitláhuac, Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies capture the last tlatoani, Cuauhtémoc, and take Tenochtitlan.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Florentine Codex by Bernardino de Sahagún, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Cortés's brigantine fleet deployed on Lake Texcoco during the siege of Tenochtitlan.

name: Inca
summary: After repelling a Chanka invasion around 1438, Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui rebuilds Cusco into an imperial capital and launches the campaigns that grow the Inca Empire into the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile and bound together by the Qhapaq Ñan road network. Huayna Capac's death from a mysterious epidemic in 1527 leaves his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fighting a ruinous civil war that Atahualpa wins only months before Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushes and captures him at Cajamarca in 1532. Atahualpa's execution and the Spanish occupation of Cusco end organized imperial rule, but a rump Neo-Inca State holds out in the mountains at Vilcabamba until Spanish forces capture the stronghold and execute its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, in 1572.
imageAttribution: Map by L'Américain, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A modern orthographic map showing the extent of the Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu, along the Andes.

events.title: Pachacuti Begins the Inca Expansion
events.body: After repelling an invasion by the rival Chanka people, Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui takes the throne, rebuilds Cusco as an imperial capital, and launches the conquests that transform a small highland kingdom into the Inca Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by an unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 18th-century portrait of Pachacuti, the ninth Sapa Inca, from a Brooklyn Museum series of paintings of Inca rulers.

events.title: Pachacuti Rebuilds the Coricancha as the Empire's Sun Temple
events.body: Pachacuti rebuilds Cusco's Coricancha, plating its walls in gold and dedicating it to Inti, the sun god; it becomes the empire's most sacred shrine and doubles as an observatory for tracking solstices and Inca constellations.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The excavated stone walls of the Coricancha, the Inca Empire's principal sun temple in Cusco.

events.title: Machu Picchu Is Built
events.body: Pachacuti commissions a royal estate high in the Andes at Machu Picchu, connected to the rest of the empire by the Qhapaq Ñan network of mountain roads and suspension bridges.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jorge Castro Ruso, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A panoramic view of the Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, built high in the Andes.

events.title: Construction Begins on the Sacsayhuamán Fortress
events.body: Pachacuti begins building the massive stone fortress of Sacsayhuamán above Cusco, a project his son Topa Inca Yupanqui and grandson Huayna Capac continue for decades using enormous interlocking limestone blocks.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The massive interlocking stone walls of Sacsayhuamán, the Inca fortress overlooking Cusco.

events.title: Topa Inca Yupanqui Conquers the Chimú Kingdom
events.body: Topa Inca Yupanqui, Pachacuti's son and successor, defeats King Minchançaman and conquers the Chimú Kingdom, the last independent state capable of rivaling the Inca on the Peruvian coast, deporting its ruler to Cusco.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A period illustration of Topa Inca Yupanqui, the tenth Sapa Inca, from Guaman Poma de Ayala's chronicle.

events.title: Huayna Capac Dies, Triggering a Succession Crisis
events.body: Emperor Huayna Capac dies at Quito of a mysterious epidemic, possibly a European disease that outran the Spanish themselves, leaving no clear heir and setting his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa on a collision course over the throne.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A period illustration by the Inca chronicler Guaman Poma de Ayala depicting Emperor Huayna Capac.

events.title: Pizarro's Expedition Makes First Contact With the Inca Empire at Tumbes
events.body: On his second voyage south, Francisco Pizarro lands at the Inca outpost of Tumbes, gathering firsthand evidence of a wealthy, organized empire that convinces the Spanish crown to authorize the conquest expedition he leads four years later.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Henry Perronet Briggs, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: Atahualpa Wins the Inca Civil War
events.body: At the Battle of Quipaipan near Cusco, Atahualpa's generals crush Huáscar's army and capture him, ending years of civil war and leaving Atahualpa in control of the empire just as Spanish forces land on the coast.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by John Harris Valda, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A painting depicting the civil war fought between the half-brothers Huáscar and Atahualpa over the Inca throne.

events.title: Atahualpa Is Captured at Cajamarca
events.body: In the town square of Cajamarca, Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushes Atahualpa's unarmed escort, massacring thousands and capturing the emperor, exploiting the recent civil war and the shock of Spanish horses and firearms.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Juan Lepiani, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A painting depicting the capture of Atahualpa by Spanish forces at the Battle of Cajamarca.

events.title: Atahualpa Is Executed
events.body: Despite paying a legendary ransom in gold and silver for his release, Atahualpa is tried and garroted at Cajamarca on charges including treason and the murder of his brother Huáscar, and Spanish forces install a puppet emperor in Cusco.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Luis Montero, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting depicting the funeral of the executed Inca emperor Atahualpa.

events.title: The Last Inti Raymi With an Inca Emperor Is Held, Then Banned
events.body: Manco Inca, the Spanish-installed puppet emperor, presides over the last Inti Raymi sun festival held with a reigning Inca before Spanish colonial authorities and Catholic priests ban the ceremony and other Inca state religious practices.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by jack_g, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern reenactment of the Inti Raymi sun festival in Cusco, with the Inca figure carried on a ceremonial throne.

events.title: Manco Inca's Rebellion Fails; the Neo-Inca State Is Founded
events.body: Manco Inca Yupanqui, installed by the Spanish as a puppet ruler, turns on his overseers and lays a ten-month siege to Cusco; when it fails, he retreats to the remote mountain refuge of Vilcabamba and founds the independent Neo-Inca State.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A period illustration by the Inca chronicler Guaman Poma de Ayala depicting Manco Inca's uprising against Spanish rule.

events.title: The Last Inca Stronghold Falls
events.body: Spanish forces capture Túpac Amaru in the forests west of Vilcabamba, march him to Cusco, and publicly behead him before thousands in the central square, ending organized Inca resistance four decades after Pizarro's first landing.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by an unidentified Cuzco School painter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Cuzco School portrait of Túpac Amaru, the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State.

name: Japan
summary: The Yamato clan's chieftains unify much of Japan from the Nara Basin around 300 AD, and over the next millennium the country moves through waves of continental influence -- Buddhism, Chinese-style law codes, and courtly aristocracy -- before military governments led by shoguns take real power from 1192 onward. Centuries of feudal warfare give way to Tokugawa unification and two and a half centuries of enforced isolation, which ends when American warships force Japan open in 1853 and the shogunate collapses in the 1868 Meiji Restoration.
imageAttribution: Photo by 663highland, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Great Buddha Hall of Tōdai-ji temple in Nara, one of Japan's most significant early Buddhist temples.

events.title: Yamato Polity Unifies the Nara Basin
events.body: Chieftains of the Yamato clan consolidate power over the Nara Basin and neighboring regions, founding the imperial line that rules Japan, at least in name, to the present day.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Immanuelle, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of ethnic groups within the early Yamato polity.

events.title: Buddhism Arrives from Baekje
events.body: King Seong of the Korean kingdom of Baekje sends Emperor Kinmei's court a Buddha image, sutras, and ritual banners, introducing Buddhism to Japan and beginning its long fusion with native Shinto practice.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Chris 73, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Asuka Great Buddha at Asuka-dera, Japan's oldest Buddhist temple, founded soon after Buddhism's introduction.

events.title: Isshi Incident Triggers the Taika Reform
events.body: Prince Naka no Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamatari assassinate the powerful minister Soga no Iruka at court, clearing the way for Emperor Kōtoku's Taika Reform, which recasts Japan's government along centralized Chinese Tang lines.
events.imageAttribution: Scroll painting by Gukei Sumiyoshi, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of the assassination of Soga no Iruka from the Tōnomine Engi scroll, painted in the Edo period.

events.title: Capital Moves to Heijō-kyō
events.body: Empress Genmei relocates Japan's capital to Heijō-kyō, a grid-planned city modeled on the Tang Chinese capital, opening the Nara period and giving Japan its first stable, permanent seat of government.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Binabik155, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the major buildings of Heijō-kyō, Japan's 8th-century capital, as it stood by the end of that century.

events.title: The Kojiki Records Japan's Origin Myths
events.body: Court scribe Ō no Yasumaro completes the Kojiki, Japan's oldest surviving chronicle, setting down the imperial line's mythic origins and oral traditions at Empress Genmei's request.
events.imageAttribution: Manuscript facsimile by Ken'yu and Koten Hozonkai, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A page from a 1920s facsimile of the 14th-century Shinpukuji manuscript of the Kojiki.

events.title: Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji Is Dedicated
events.body: Emperor Shōmu presides over the eye-opening ceremony for Tōdai-ji's Great Buddha, a colossal bronze statue built to anchor a nationwide network of Buddhist temples and project imperial authority through faith.
events.imageAttribution: Rubbing by an anonymous artist, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1930-published rubbing of an incised bronze lotus petal from the Great Buddha's original 752 pedestal.

events.title: Capital Moves to Heian-kyō
events.body: Emperor Kanmu relocates the capital to Heian-kyō, opening the four-century Heian period in which a hereditary court aristocracy presides over a golden age of Japanese literature and art.
events.imageAttribution: Illustrated scroll from The Tale of Genji, Imperial court in Kyoto, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A scene from the illustrated Tale of Genji handscroll (Genji Monogatari Emaki), an early 12th-century work depicting Heian court life.

events.title: Murasaki Shikibu Writes The Tale of Genji
events.body: Court lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu completes The Tale of Genji around the height of the Heian period, a sweeping court romance widely regarded as the world's first novel and a landmark of Japanese prose.
events.imageAttribution: Scroll fragment, artist likely Fujiwara Takachika or Takayoshi, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 12th-century illustrated scroll fragment (Genji Monogatari Emaki) depicting a scene from The Tale of Genji, held at the Gotoh Museum.

events.title: Battle of Dan-no-ura Ends the Genpei War
events.body: The Minamoto fleet annihilates the Taira clan's navy in the Kanmon Strait, drowning the child emperor Antoku with it and ending the five-year Genpei War that clears Minamoto no Yoritomo's path to founding the Kamakura shogunate.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Tosa Mitsunobu, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A scroll painting depicting the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura, from the illustrated biography of Emperor Antoku.

events.title: Eisai Introduces Zen Buddhism
events.body: The monk Myōan Eisai returns from studying in China and founds Shōfuku-ji, Japan's first Zen temple, introducing the Rinzai school that becomes deeply entwined with the later samurai class.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of the Zen monk Eisai, founder of Japan's Rinzai school.

events.title: Minamoto no Yoritomo Becomes Shogun
events.body: Minamoto no Yoritomo receives the title of shogun from the emperor, formalizing the military government he had already built at Kamakura and beginning nearly seven centuries of rule by warrior-class shoguns rather than the imperial court.
events.imageAttribution: Woodblock print by Utagawa Sadahide, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1862 print depicting Minamoto no Yoritomo's procession into Kyoto, around 1190.

events.title: Kamikaze Repel the Second Mongol Invasion
events.body: A typhoon destroys Kublai Khan's invasion fleet off Kyushu for the second time in seven years, ending Mongol attempts to conquer Japan and giving rise to the legend of the kamikaze, or "divine wind."
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Qiushufang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the two Mongol invasion routes into Japan in 1274 and 1281.

events.title: Kenmu Restoration Ends the Kamakura Shogunate
events.body: Emperor Go-Daigo, backed by defecting warlords Ashikaga Takauji and Nitta Yoshisada, topples the Kamakura shogunate and briefly restores direct imperial rule, an arrangement that collapses within three years into renewed civil war.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by Monkan-bō Kōshin, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Emperor Go-Daigo, who led the Kenmu Restoration against the Kamakura shogunate.

events.title: Ashikaga Takauji Becomes Shogun
events.body: Ashikaga Takauji, having turned on Emperor Go-Daigo and installed a rival imperial line, receives the title of shogun and founds the Ashikaga shogunate, opening the Muromachi period.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait traditionally identified as Ashikaga Takauji, founder of the Ashikaga shogunate.

events.title: Kinkaku-ji Rises as a Symbol of Muromachi Culture
events.body: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu converts a Kyoto villa into Kinkaku-ji, the gold-leafed Golden Pavilion, embodying the refined Kitayama culture that flourishes under Ashikaga patronage.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Nacaru, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Golden Pavilion of Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto, reflected in its surrounding pond.

events.title: Ōnin War Shatters Central Authority
events.body: A succession dispute among the shogunate's leading families erupts into a decade of fighting centered on Kyoto, permanently weakening the Ashikaga shogunate and opening the Sengoku, or "Warring States," era of rival regional daimyo.
events.imageAttribution: Woodblock print by Utagawa Yoshitora, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Battle of Ōnin during the Ōnin War (1467-1477), depicted by Utagawa Yoshitora.

events.title: Francis Xavier Introduces Christianity
events.body: Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier lands at Kagoshima to open the first Christian mission in Japan, beginning nearly a century of missionary activity that Tokugawa rulers later move to suppress.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from a Japanese history volume covering the Kamakura through Sengoku periods, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of the Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier.

events.title: Oda Nobunaga Topples the Ashikaga Shogunate
events.body: Oda Nobunaga expels shogun Ashikaga Yoshiaki from Kyoto, ending the 237-year Ashikaga shogunate and launching his campaign of forcible reunification that Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu later complete.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by Kanō Sōshū, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of the warlord Oda Nobunaga.

events.title: Hideyoshi Orders the Sword Hunt
events.body: Toyotomi Hideyoshi decrees a nationwide sword hunt disarming the peasantry, a foundational step in fixing a rigid separation between the warrior and farming classes that endures through the Edo period.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by Kanō Mitsunobu, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1598 portrait of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, held at Kōdai-ji Temple in Kyoto.

events.title: Japan Invades Korea
events.body: Toyotomi Hideyoshi launches a massive invasion of Korea aimed ultimately at conquering Ming China, opening six years of brutal warfare across the peninsula before ending in Japanese withdrawal.
events.imageAttribution: Painting, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of the Japanese siege of Busanjin fortress, the opening battle of the 1592 invasion.

events.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu Wins at Sekigahara
events.body: Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern Army crushes the rival Western coalition at Sekigahara, a victory that ends over a century of civil war and, three years later, brings him the title of shogun, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that rules Japan for the next two and a half centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Folding screen painting, Collection of the Town of Sekigahara Archive of History and Cultural Anthropology, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A folding screen (byōbu) depicting the Battle of Sekigahara, based on an early 17th-century original.

events.title: Izumo no Okuni Originates Kabuki
events.body: The performer Izumo no Okuni stages a new style of dance-drama on the dry bed of Kyoto's Kamo River, giving rise to kabuki theater the same year Tokugawa Ieyasu establishes his shogunate.
events.imageAttribution: Screen painting, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Izumo no Okuni from the six-panel Okuni Kabuki-zu Byōbu screen, held at the Kyoto National Museum.

events.title: Shimabara Rebellion Erupts
events.body: Persecuted Christian and peasant rebels seize Hara Castle in a months-long uprising against crushing taxation and religious suppression, the largest civil conflict of the Edo period and the last major armed rebellion before centuries of Tokugawa peace.
events.imageAttribution: Map, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century map depicting the siege of Hara Castle during the Shimabara Rebellion.

events.title: Sakoku Edict Seals Japan's Borders
events.body: The Tokugawa shogunate issues its final seclusion edict, expelling the Portuguese and confining nearly all foreign trade to a single Dutch outpost, closing Japan to the outside world for more than two centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Isaac Titsingh, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A ground plan of Dejima, the artificial island in Nagasaki harbor that became Japan's sole window to the West under sakoku.

events.title: Kaitai Shinsho Introduces Western Medicine
