events.body: Physician Sugita Genpaku publishes Kaitai Shinsho, a translation of a Dutch anatomical text, launching Rangaku -- the study of Western science smuggled in through Japan's single open port at Nagasaki.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Babi Hijau, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: Ōshio Heihachirō's Rebellion
events.body: Former police official and Confucian scholar Ōshio Heihachirō leads an uprising in Osaka to protest the shogunate's failure to relieve famine, briefly setting the merchant district ablaze before being crushed within a day.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by Kikuchi Yōsai, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Ōshio Heihachirō, held in the Osaka Castle Museum collection.

events.title: Commodore Perry Forces Japan Open
events.body: US Commodore Matthew Perry sails a squadron of warships into Uraga, forcing the Tokugawa shogunate to abandon over two centuries of sakoku isolation and open Japanese ports to American trade.
events.imageAttribution: Japanese print, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1854 Japanese print of Commodore Perry's fleet, showing one of the two paddlewheel steamers on his visit.

events.title: Meiji Restoration Ends the Shogunate
events.body: Emperor Meiji is restored to direct political power and the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, surrenders his authority, ending nearly 700 years of shogunate rule and launching Japan's rapid modernization.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Takahashi Yuichi, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Emperor Meiji by Takahashi Yuichi, held in the Imperial Collection.

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: The Ottoman Empire grows from a small Turkoman frontier principality founded by Osman I around 1299 into a vast Islamic empire spanning Europe, Asia, and North Africa -- conquering Constantinople in 1453, claiming the Islamic caliphate after Selim I's 1517 conquest of the Mamluks, and reaching its territorial and cultural height under Suleiman the Magnificent and the 18th-century Tulip Era. Centuries of slow retreat follow -- the loss of Greece, sweeping 19th-century reform and constitutional efforts, and the near-total loss of its remaining territory in the Balkan Wars and World War I -- before the Grand National Assembly abolishes the sultanate in 1922.
imageAttribution: Map by Chamboz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Ottoman Empire's territorial extent in 1683, near its greatest reach.

events.title: Osman I Founds the Ottoman Beylik
events.body: Osman I, a Turkoman frontier lord ruling from the small Anatolian town of Söğüt, breaks from Seljuk overlordship and founds the beylik that will grow into the Ottoman Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Ottoman miniature painting, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Ottoman miniature portrait of Osman I, founder of the Ottoman Empire.

events.title: Mehmed II Conquers Constantinople
events.body: Sultan Mehmed II breaches Constantinople's ancient walls after a 53-day siege using massive cannon, ending the Byzantine Empire and transforming Ottoman rule from a regional power into an empire straddling Europe and Asia.
events.imageAttribution: Fresco, Moldovita Monastery, photo by DimiTalen, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern fresco at Moldovita Monastery in Romania depicting the siege of Constantinople.

events.title: Selim I Conquers the Mamluk Sultanate and Claims the Caliphate
events.body: Sultan Selim I crushes the Mamluk Sultanate at the Battle of Ridaniya and captures Cairo, absorbing Egypt, Syria, and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina into Ottoman territory and transferring the Islamic caliphate's religious authority to the Ottoman throne.
events.imageAttribution: 16th-century Basel news pamphlet (1518), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1518 Basel news pamphlet documenting the Ottoman conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate and Mecca and Medina.

events.title: Suleiman the Magnificent Besieges Vienna
events.body: Suleiman the Magnificent lays siege to the Habsburg capital of Vienna but withdraws after 18 days when rain, dwindling supplies, and the approaching winter make the walls unbreakable in time -- marking the deepest advance of Ottoman power into Central Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Bartel Beham, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A contemporary engraving depicting the 1529 Ottoman siege of Vienna.

events.title: Mimar Sinan Completes the Süleymaniye Mosque
events.body: Imperial architect Mimar Sinan completes the Süleymaniye Mosque on Istanbul's Third Hill, a domed complex commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent that becomes the empire's grandest architectural expression of its classical-age power.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Hunanuk, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent.

events.title: The Holy League Destroys the Ottoman Fleet at Lepanto
events.body: A Holy League fleet of Spanish, Venetian, and papal galleys crushes the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras, ending decades of unchallenged Ottoman dominance at sea even as the empire rebuilds its fleet within a year.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Laureys a Castro, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century painting depicting the naval Battle of Lepanto.

events.title: Taqi al-Din Founds the Istanbul Observatory
events.body: Astronomer Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ma'ruf establishes an observatory in Istanbul rivaling the great observatories of the era, equipping it with instruments of his own design before conservative religious opposition leads to its demolition just three years later.
events.imageAttribution: Miniature painting by Ala ad-Din Mansur-Shirazi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A miniature from the Şehinşahname depicting Ottoman astronomers at work at the Istanbul Observatory under Taqi al-Din.

events.title: The Ottomans Are Routed at the Battle of Vienna
events.body: A relief army led by Polish king John III Sobieski smashes the two-month Ottoman siege of Vienna, halting the empire's westward expansion for good and touching off a sixteen-year war that steadily rolls back Ottoman territory in Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Painting, Museum of Military History Vienna, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A monumental painting depicting the 1683 siege and relief of Vienna.

events.title: The Treaty of Karlowitz Ends the Great Turkish War
events.body: Defeated in the Great Turkish War, the Ottoman Empire signs the Treaty of Karlowitz, ceding Hungary and other territories to the Habsburgs, Podolia to Poland-Lithuania, and Dalmatia and the Morea to Venice in its first major territorial retreat from a coalition of European powers.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by O.Mustafin, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A copy of the Treaty of Karlowitz document exhibited in the Doge's Palace in Venice.

events.title: The Tulip Era Ushers in a Golden Age of Ottoman Art
events.body: Following the Treaty of Passarowitz, Sultan Ahmed III and Grand Vizier Nevşehirli Damat İbrahim Pasha open the Tulip Era, a period of relative peace marked by lavish gardens, Westward-looking court culture, and a flourishing of miniature painting and architecture in Istanbul.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Julien Maury, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Ahmed III Fountain in Istanbul, a landmark built during the Tulip Era.

events.title: İbrahim Müteferrika Opens the First Ottoman Printing Press
events.body: Hungarian-born convert İbrahim Müteferrika receives a sultanic decree to establish the first printing press to use movable Arabic type in the Muslim world, publishing works on history, geography, and science from his Istanbul workshop.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of a statue by Ogodej, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A statue of İbrahim Müteferrika in Istanbul, near the Grand Bazaar.

events.title: The Patrona Halil Revolt Ends the Tulip Era
events.body: A former janissary named Patrona Halil leads a mob uprising through Istanbul that forces Sultan Ahmed III to abdicate in favor of Mahmud I, ending the Tulip Era's cultural experimentation amid a conservative backlash against its costly extravagance.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Jean Baptiste Vanmour, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Patrona Halil leading the 1730 uprising that ended the Tulip Era.

events.title: The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca Marks the Empire's First Major Retreat
events.body: Defeated by Russia after a six-year war, the Ottoman Empire signs the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, recognizing Crimean independence and granting Russia the right to intervene on behalf of Orthodox Christians within Ottoman territory -- a precedent later powers repeatedly invoke to justify meddling in Ottoman affairs.
events.imageAttribution: Allegorical 18th-century engraving, Cabinet of Engravings of the Romanian Academy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A contemporary allegorical engraving depicting the Ottoman Empire losing territory under the 1774 treaty.

events.title: Mahmud II Abolishes the Janissary Corps in the Auspicious Incident
events.body: Sultan Mahmud II crushes a janissary mutiny in Istanbul and forcibly disbands the centuries-old corps, clearing the way for a modern, European-style army and consolidating central authority after decades of janissary interference in politics.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Christoph Weigel the Elder and Caspar Luyken, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1703 engraving depicting an Ottoman janissary, the corps abolished in the Auspicious Incident.

events.title: The London Protocol Recognizes Greek Independence
events.body: After nearly a decade of revolt across the Greek peninsula, the London Protocol formally recognizes Greece as an independent state, marking the Ottoman Empire's first loss of a subject nation to nationalist revolution.
events.imageAttribution: Fresco by Ludwig Michael von Schwanthaler, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A fresco in the Greek Parliament's Trophy Hall depicting the signing of the London Protocol.

events.title: The Edict of Gülhane Launches the Tanzimat Reforms
events.body: Sultan Abdülmecid I proclaims the Edict of Gülhane at Topkapı Palace, launching the Tanzimat era of reforms that overhaul Ottoman law, education, and taxation in an attempt to modernize the empire and halt its long decline.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by David Wilkie, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Sultan Abdülmecid I, who proclaimed the Edict of Gülhane.

events.title: The Ottoman Empire Adopts Its First Constitution
events.body: Sultan Abdul Hamid II promulgates the empire's first written constitution, establishing an elected parliament and opening the First Constitutional Era before suspending it just two years later amid war with Russia.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from The Graphic (1877), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The first meeting of the Ottoman Parliament in Constantinople, March 1877.

events.title: The Congress of Berlin Strips the Ottomans of Balkan Territory
events.body: European powers meeting in Berlin revise the harsh terms Russia imposed after the Russo-Turkish War, but still force the Ottoman Empire to cede vast Balkan territory and recognize the independence of Serbia, Montenegro, and Romania.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Anton von Werner, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1892 painting depicting the Congress of Berlin of July 1878.

events.title: The Young Turk Revolution Restores the Constitution
events.body: Army officers of the Committee of Union and Progress rise up in Ottoman Macedonia and force Sultan Abdul Hamid II to restore the suspended 1876 constitution, ending three decades of autocratic rule and opening the empire's final constitutional era.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Charles Roden Buxton, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Religious leaders of different faiths appearing together to mark the 1908 constitutional restoration.

events.title: The Balkan Wars Strip the Ottomans of Nearly All European Territory
events.body: Defeated by a coalition of Balkan states in the First Balkan War, the Ottoman Empire signs the Treaty of London, ceding almost all its remaining European provinces and the Aegean islands -- reducing six centuries of Ottoman Europe to a small strip of Eastern Thrace.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The signing of the Treaty of London on 30 May 1913, ending the First Balkan War.

events.title: The Gallipoli Campaign Repels an Allied Invasion
events.body: Ottoman forces under commanders including Mustafa Kemal successfully defend the Gallipoli Peninsula against a nine-month Allied invasion aimed at capturing Constantinople, inflicting a costly defeat that boosts Ottoman morale and launches Mustafa Kemal's rise to prominence.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by George Washington Lambert, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Australian troops landing at Anzac Cove during the Gallipoli campaign, April 1915.

events.title: Ottoman Authorities Launch the Armenian Genocide
events.body: Ottoman authorities arrest and deport hundreds of Armenian intellectuals from Constantinople on April 24, 1915, beginning a systematic campaign of massacre and forced deportation that kills hundreds of thousands to over a million Armenians by the war's end.
events.imageAttribution: Photograph published in Ravished Armenia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A column of Armenian deportees being marched through the Harput region during the genocide.

events.title: The Grand National Assembly Abolishes the Sultanate
events.body: The Grand National Assembly in Ankara abolishes the Ottoman sultanate, stripping Sultan Mehmed VI of political power and formally ending over six centuries of Ottoman rule as the last sultan departs Constantinople into exile.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Sultan Mehmed VI departing Dolmabahçe Palace shortly before his exile in November 1922.

name: Vikings (Norse)
summary: Norse seafarers from Scandinavia erupt onto the European stage with the 793 raid on Lindisfarne, launching two and a half centuries of raiding, trading, and settlement that reaches from North America to the Caspian Sea. Along the way Norsemen found or seize territory as far apart as Dublin, Normandy, and Novgorod, unify Norway and Denmark into lasting kingdoms, and briefly rule an English throne, before the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066 marks the traditional close of the Viking Age.
imageAttribution: Photo by the Swedish History Museum, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A Viking-age picture stone from Smiss on the island of Gotland, Sweden, carved with scenes typical of Norse art.

events.title: Vikings Raid the Monastery at Lindisfarne
events.body: Norse raiders sack the undefended monastery on the island of Lindisfarne, killing and enslaving monks and looting its treasures. The attack shocks Christian Europe and is conventionally treated as the opening event of the Viking Age.
events.imageAttribution: Illuminated manuscript page attributed to Eadfrith of Lindisfarne, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A page from the Lindisfarne Gospels, the monastery's most famous surviving work, produced not long before the raid.

events.title: The Oseberg Ship Burial
events.body: A richly furnished ship burial at Oseberg near Tønsberg interns two women, likely a high-status woman and a companion, alongside carved sleighs, a wagon, and textiles worked in the ornate Viking "gripping beast" style. Excavated in 1904, it remains the best-preserved trove of Viking Age art and craftsmanship yet found.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Petter Ulleland, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The excavated Oseberg ship on display at the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo.

events.title: Vikings Found a Longphort at Dublin
events.body: Norse raiders establish a fortified base, a longphort, on the River Liffey, giving them a permanent foothold in Ireland for the first time. The camp grows into Dublin, which becomes the leading Norse settlement in Ireland.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Yorkshirian, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Viking-era settlements and raid sites in Ireland.

events.title: Rurik Founds the Rus' State at Novgorod
events.body: The Varangian chieftain Rurik is invited to rule at Novgorod, founding the line of princes later credited with establishing the Rus' state. His successors carry the dynasty south to Kiev, laying the groundwork for medieval Russia and Ukraine.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Дар Ветер, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Rurik depicted on the Millennium of Russia monument in Veliky Novgorod.

events.title: The Great Heathen Army Invades England
events.body: A large coalition of Scandinavian warriors lands in East Anglia and begins a sustained campaign of conquest, unlike the earlier hit-and-run raids. Within a decade it topples three of England's four Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and carves out the Danelaw.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Hel-hama, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Great Heathen Army's campaign routes across Anglo-Saxon England.

events.title: Harald Fairhair Unifies Norway at Hafrsfjord
events.body: Harald defeats a coalition of rival chieftains at the Battle of Hafrsfjord near Stavanger, becoming the first king to rule all of Norway. Tradition holds that many defeated chieftains flee overseas, fueling the settlement of Iceland.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Ole Peter Hansen Balling, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of Harald Fairhair at the Battle of Hafrsfjord.

events.title: Ingólfr Arnarson Settles Iceland
events.body: Ingólfr Arnarson establishes the first permanent Norse settlement at Reykjavík, traditionally marking the start of Iceland's Age of Settlement. Within decades the island holds a Norse population governed by its own assembly, the Althing.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Oscar Wergeland, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting imagining Norse settlers landing in Iceland.

events.title: Alfred the Great Defeats Guthrum at Edington
events.body: King Alfred of Wessex routs Guthrum's Great Heathen Army at Edington in Wiltshire, reversing years of Viking advances after months in hiding at Athelney. Guthrum accepts baptism and the Treaty of Wedmore, fixing the boundary that becomes the Danelaw and securing Wessex as the last independent Anglo-Saxon kingdom.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Trish Steel, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A memorial stone marking the site of the Battle of Edington near Bratton Castle, Wiltshire.

events.title: Rollo Founds the Duchy of Normandy
events.body: The West Frankish king cedes land around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo in exchange for peace and nominal loyalty, founding the Duchy of Normandy. Rollo's Norse followers intermarry with the local population, and his descendants later conquer England as Normans.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Rollo, Duke of Normandy, depicted on a medieval roll of the dukes of Normandy.

events.title: Icelandic Settlers Found the Althing at Þingvellir
events.body: Iceland's free settlers convene the first Althing at Þingvellir, adopting a law code carried back from Norway by Úlfljótr and establishing an annual assembly where chieftains legislate and settle disputes at the Lögberg, the Law Rock. The gathering is often cited as the world's oldest surviving parliament.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by W. G. Collingwood, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A romanticized depiction of the Althing in session at Þingvellir.

events.title: Harald Bluetooth Christianizes Denmark
events.body: King Harald Gormsson raises a runestone at Jelling proclaiming that he made the Danes Christian, formally converting his kingdom. The stone becomes an enduring symbol of Denmark's unification and religious transformation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Alicudi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Jelling stones, raised by Harald Bluetooth to commemorate his parents and Denmark's conversion to Christianity.

events.title: Byzantine Emperor Basil II Forms the Varangian Guard
events.body: In exchange for military aid against rebellious generals, Byzantine emperor Basil II receives 6,000 Rus' warriors from Vladimir I of Kiev and forms them into an elite imperial bodyguard, the Varangian Guard. Recruited from Scandinavia and Rus' lands with no local political ties, the unit serves Byzantine emperors for over three centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of the Piraeus Lion, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Piraeus Lion in Venice, carved with runes describing Swedish warriors, likely Varangians, serving the Byzantine emperor.

events.title: Leif Erikson Reaches Vinland
events.body: Sailing west from Greenland, Leif Erikson becomes the first European known to reach North America, naming the land Vinland. A Norse camp excavated at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, with wood tree-ring dated to the early 11th century, confirms Norse presence in the region.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Dylan Kereluk, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstructed Norse longhouse at the L'Anse aux Meadows site in Newfoundland, Canada.

events.title: Iceland Adopts Christianity by Vote of the Althing
events.body: Facing a split between Christian and pagan factions that threatens civil war, the lawspeaker Thorgeir Ljósvetningagoði persuades the Althing to accept Christianity as Iceland's official religion in exchange for tolerating private pagan worship. Tradition holds that Thorgeir casts his own idols into the Goðafoss waterfall afterward.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Andreas Tille, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Goðafoss, the waterfall where Thorgeir is said to have cast his pagan idols after Iceland's conversion.

events.title: Brian Boru Breaks Viking Power at Clontarf
events.body: High King Brian Boru's army defeats a Dublin-Leinster alliance backed by Viking forces from Orkney and the Isle of Man near Dublin, though Brian is killed after the fighting ends. The battle shatters the political dominance of the Norse kingdom of Dublin, which never again rules as an independent power in Ireland.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Hugh Frazer, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1826 oil painting depicting the Battle of Clontarf.

events.title: Cnut Becomes King of England
events.body: After defeating Edmund Ironside's army at the Battle of Assandun, Cnut is accepted as king of all England following Edmund's death weeks later. He goes on to rule Denmark and Norway as well, forging the short-lived North Sea Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Illuminated manuscript, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Cnut depicted in the Liber Vitae of New Minster, Winchester, 1031.

events.title: The Battle of Stamford Bridge Ends the Viking Age
events.body: King Harold Godwinson's army destroys an invading Norwegian force, killing King Harald Hardrada in the fighting. The defeat ends serious Scandinavian ambitions to conquer England and is conventionally treated as the close of the Viking Age.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Matthew Paris, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th-century depiction of the Battle of Stamford Bridge from Matthew Paris's Life of King Edward the Confessor.

name: Mughal Empire
summary: The Mughal Empire ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to 1857, beginning when the Central Asian conqueror Babur toppled the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat. It reached its cultural and territorial peak under Akbar, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb, leaving behind monuments like the Taj Mahal, before Persian invasion and British expansion reduced its later emperors to figureheads and ended the dynasty after the 1857 rebellion.
imageAttribution: Map by Charles Joppen, from A Historical Atlas of India (1907), PD-US, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: Map of India circa 1700 showing the Mughal Empire's extent alongside European trading posts.

events.title: Babur Founds the Mughal Empire at Panipat
events.body: Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, defeats the Delhi Sultanate's Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat using cannon and matchlock muskets that Indian armies haven't yet faced, then takes Delhi and Agra to found the Mughal Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Painting from the Baburnama, artist unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Illustration from Babur's memoirs depicting the First Battle of Panipat and the death of Sultan Ibrahim Lodi.

events.title: Sher Shah Suri Defeats Humayun, Launching the Sur Interregnum
events.body: Sher Shah Suri, an Afghan noble turned rebel, crushes Babur's son and successor Humayun at the Battle of Kannauj, driving him into 15 years of exile in Persia and replacing Mughal rule in Delhi with his own Sur Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Mughal-era manuscript painting from the Tarikh-i-Khandan-i-Timuriya, artist unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: Akbar Wins the Second Battle of Panipat, Restoring Mughal Rule
events.body: A year after Humayun reclaims Delhi with Safavid Persian help and then dies in a fall, his 13-year-old son Akbar, guided by regent Bairam Khan, defeats the Hindu king Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat, securing the throne and opening a 50-year reign that consolidates Mughal control over most of the subcontinent.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Kankar from the Akbarnama, c. 1590s, National Gallery of Victoria, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The defeat of Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat, depicted in a painting from the Akbarnama.

events.title: Akbar Promulgates the Din-i-Ilahi
events.body: At the height of his power, Akbar introduces the Din-i-Ilahi, a syncretic court order blending elements of Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, and Christianity, reflecting his broader policy of religious tolerance toward an empire whose subjects are overwhelmingly non-Muslim.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait of Akbar, artist unknown, Museum of Fine Arts Boston, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Emperor Akbar holding a falcon.

events.title: Thomas Roe's Embassy Gives the English a Foothold at Surat
events.body: English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe arrives at Jahangir's court, where he spends three years failing to win major trading privileges but does secure permission for an East India Company factory at Surat -- the toehold from which British commercial presence in India eventually grows.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait of Thomas Roe, after Michiel Jansz. van Mierevelt, National Portrait Gallery, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Portrait of Thomas Roe, English ambassador to the Mughal court.

events.title: Shah Jahan Commissions the Taj Mahal
events.body: Grieving the death of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan commissions an ivory-white marble mausoleum at Agra; the main structure is finished by 1648 and the surrounding complex by 1653, becoming the signature monument of the empire's cultural peak.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Yann Forget, edited by Jim Carter, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Taj Mahal at Agra.

events.title: Aurangzeb Conquers Golconda, the Empire Reaches Its Greatest Extent
events.body: After an eight-month siege, Aurangzeb's army takes the fortress of Golconda from the Qutb Shahi dynasty, completing his conquest of the last independent Deccan sultanates -- Bijapur fell the year before -- and pushing Mughal borders across nearly the entire Indian subcontinent, the empire's largest territorial extent.
events.imageAttribution: Gouache painting from the Anne S.K. Brown Military Collection, artist unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Emperor Aurangzeb, carried on a litter, directs the siege of Golconda in 1687.

events.title: Nader Shah Sacks Delhi
events.body: The Persian conqueror Nader Shah crushes a much larger Mughal army and occupies Delhi, carrying off the imperial treasury including the jewel-encrusted Peacock Throne -- a blow so severe the empire never fully recovers its former wealth or authority.
events.imageAttribution: Painting of Nader Shah in the Red Fort, artist unknown, c. 1739, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Nader Shah depicted enthroned in Delhi's Red Fort as a Mughal-style emperor, circa 1739.

events.title: The British Win Bengal at the Battle of Plassey
events.body: Robert Clive's East India Company force defeats the Nawab of Bengal after bribing his own commander into betrayal, giving the Company effective control of the empire's richest province and marking the start of British political dominance in India.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Francis Hayman, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: The Mughal Empire Ends With the 1857 Rebellion
events.body: Indian soldiers rebelling against East India Company rule proclaim the aged Bahadur Shah II their symbolic leader in Delhi; after crushing the rebellion the British capture and depose him, later trying and exiling him to Rangoon, ending 331 years of Mughal dynastic rule.
events.imageAttribution: Photograph of Bahadur Shah II, photographer unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Portrait of Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal emperor.

name: Holy Roman Empire
summary: Founded when Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans in 800, the empire coalesces into its lasting form under the Ottonian dynasty, whose Otto I is crowned emperor in 962 after breaking a Magyar army at Lechfeld. Popes and emperors spend the next two centuries locked in the Investiture Controversy over who appoints bishops, a conflict that reaches its most humbling moment at Canossa and its formal end at the Concordat of Worms, while the Hohenstaufen emperors Frederick Barbarossa and Frederick II clash with the papacy and Italy's city-states before the dynasty's collapse plunges the empire into the Great Interregnum. Rudolf I's 1273 election restores order and begins the House of Habsburg's long grip on the imperial title, formalized by Charles IV's Golden Bull and Maximilian I's Imperial Reform -- even as Gutenberg's printing press at Mainz and Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg set off a Reformation that fractures the empire's religious unity and, after the catastrophic Thirty Years' War, leaves its central authority increasingly nominal. The empire limps on as a loose confederation of hundreds of states until Napoleon's pressure forces Francis II to dissolve it on 6 August 1806.
imageAttribution: Map by ziegelbrenner, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Holy Roman Empire's territories in 1648, near the end of the Thirty Years' War.

events.title: Charlemagne Is Crowned Emperor
events.body: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne "Emperor of the Romans" at St. Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day, reviving the Western imperial title and giving the later Holy Roman Empire its founding, legendary predecessor.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval depiction of Pope Leo III crowning Charlemagne emperor.

events.title: The Palatine Chapel at Aachen Is Consecrated
events.body: Charlemagne's octagonal chapel at his palace in Aachen is consecrated by Pope Leo III, becoming the burial place of Carolingian and later emperors and a model for imperial church architecture across the empire's history.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Lokilech, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The octagonal core of Charlemagne's Palatine Chapel at Aachen.

events.title: The Treaty of Verdun Creates East Francia
events.body: Charlemagne's three grandsons divide the Carolingian Empire at Verdun; Louis the German takes the eastern lands beyond the Rhine that grow into the medieval Kingdom of Germany, the core territory the Holy Roman Empire is built on.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Louis the Pious blesses the three-way division of the Carolingian Empire in 843.

events.title: Otto I Crushes the Magyars at Lechfeld
events.body: King Otto I annihilates a Magyar raiding army on the Lechfeld plain outside Augsburg, ending decades of Magyar incursions into Western Europe and building the military prestige that leads to his imperial coronation seven years later.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Hektor Mülich, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 15th-century illustration of the Battle of Lechfeld.

events.title: Otto I Is Crowned Holy Roman Emperor
events.body: Pope John XII crowns Otto I emperor in Rome, reviving Charlemagne's imperial title after a nearly 40-year vacancy and founding the continuous line of emperors that historians treat as the Holy Roman Empire proper.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Otto Posse, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The imperial seal of Otto I.

events.title: Archbishop Gero Commissions the Gero Cross
events.body: Archbishop Gero of Cologne commissions a large wooden crucifix showing Christ dead rather than alive on the cross, the oldest surviving large-scale sculpture of the crucifixion in the West and a landmark of Ottonian religious art.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Elya, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Gero Cross, the oldest known large Western sculpture of the crucified Christ.

events.title: Henry IV Walks to Canossa
events.body: Facing excommunication and a revolt of German princes, Emperor Henry IV travels to Canossa Castle and stands penitent in the snow for three days until Pope Gregory VII lifts his excommunication, the most humbling moment of the Investiture Controversy over who controls the appointment of bishops.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Eduard Schwoiser, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of Henry IV's penitent journey to Canossa.

events.title: The Concordat of Worms Ends the Investiture Controversy
events.body: Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II sign a compromise at Worms separating a bishop's spiritual authority, granted by the Church, from his secular authority as a landholder, granted by the emperor, closing five decades of conflict over who appoints Church officials.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of the original document, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The original charter of the Concordat of Worms.

events.title: Frederick Barbarossa Is Crowned Emperor
events.body: Pope Adrian IV crowns Frederick I "Barbarossa" emperor in Rome, beginning the reign of the Hohenstaufen dynasty's most famous ruler, who spends much of his 35-year reign trying to reassert imperial authority over northern Italy.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Montecappio, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gilded bronze bust of Frederick Barbarossa, cast around 1160.

events.title: The Lombard League Defeats Barbarossa at Legnano
events.body: A coalition of northern Italian city-states known as the Lombard League routs Frederick Barbarossa's imperial army at Legnano, proving communal militias could beat imperial knights and forcing the emperor to recognize the cities' self-government.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Amos Cassioli, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of the Battle of Legnano.

events.title: Frederick II Founds the University of Naples
events.body: Emperor Frederick II, a patron of science known for his own treatise on falconry, charters the University of Naples as a state-funded institution independent of the Church, one of the first universities in the world established by royal rather than papal authority.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Frederick II depicted with a falcon in his own treatise on hunting with birds.

events.title: Construction Begins on Cologne Cathedral
events.body: Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden lays the foundation stone for a new Gothic cathedral at Cologne, an undertaking so ambitious that construction stalls for centuries and the building isn't finished until 1880, decades after the empire that began it had ceased to exist.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The west facade of Cologne Cathedral.

events.title: Frederick II's Death Begins the Great Interregnum
events.body: Frederick II dies at Castel Fiorentino in southern Italy, and without an emperor able to command wide recognition, the empire drifts for over two decades of rival kings and civil war remembered as the Great Interregnum.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by an unknown copyist (Diebold Lauber workshop), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 15th-century manuscript illustration titled "The Interregnum: Three Men at the Grave of an Emperor."

events.title: Rudolf I of Habsburg Is Elected King, Ending the Interregnum
events.body: The prince-electors unanimously choose the minor Swabian count Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans at Frankfurt, ending 23 years without a widely recognized ruler and beginning the House of Habsburg's rise to become the empire's dominant dynasty.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Wolfgang Sauber, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The seal of Rudolf I of Habsburg.

events.title: Charles IV Founds Charles University in Prague
events.body: Emperor Charles IV persuades Pope Clement VI to charter a university at Prague modeled on the University of Paris, founding the first university in Central Europe and turning his capital into a major center of medieval learning.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Packare, of a 14th-century Bohemian manuscript facsimile, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of a class in medieval Bohemia from a late 14th-century manuscript.

events.title: The Golden Bull Fixes the Empire's Constitution
events.body: Emperor Charles IV issues the Golden Bull, formally naming seven prince-electors -- three archbishops and four secular rulers -- with the sole right to elect future emperors, a framework for choosing the empire's ruler that holds for over four centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of the original document, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A close-up of the sealed Golden Bull of 1356.

events.title: Gutenberg Completes the Printed Bible at Mainz
events.body: Johannes Gutenberg finishes printing roughly 180 copies of a Latin Bible in Mainz using movable metal type, the first major book produced this way and the breakthrough that makes mass-produced, identical books possible across Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by NYC Wanderer (Kevin Eng), CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A copy of the Gutenberg Bible held at the New York Public Library.

events.title: The Diet of Worms Enacts the Imperial Reform
events.body: Emperor Maximilian I and the Imperial Diet at Worms ban private feuding between the empire's territories, create an Imperial Chamber Court to settle disputes by law, and levy the empire's first general tax, an attempt to turn a loose patchwork of states into a functioning central government.
events.imageAttribution: Stamp design by Deutsche Bundespost, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A West German postage stamp commemorating the 1495 Diet of Worms.

events.title: Martin Luther Publishes the Ninety-five Theses
events.body: Martin Luther, a theology professor at Wittenberg, circulates ninety-five propositions attacking the Church's sale of indulgences, a challenge that spreads rapidly once it's printed and touches off the Reformation that splits the empire's religious unity.
events.imageAttribution: Document by Martin Luther, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A printed copy of Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses.

events.title: The Diet of Worms Outlaws Martin Luther
events.body: Summoned before Emperor Charles V and the Imperial Diet at Worms, Luther refuses to recant his writings; the emperor responds with the Edict of Worms, declaring him a heretic and outlaw and banning the spread of his ideas across the empire.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Anton von Werner, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of Martin Luther before the Diet of Worms.

events.title: Peasant Armies Are Crushed at Frankenhausen
events.body: Preacher Thomas Müntzer leads thousands of peasants into battle at Frankenhausen, the final major engagement of the German Peasants' War; the poorly armed rebels are slaughtered by the forces of Hesse and Saxony, part of a wider revolt whose defeat costs an estimated 100,000 peasant lives across the empire.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An engraving of the final battle of the German Peasants' War at Frankenhausen.

events.title: Dürer Paints The Four Apostles
events.body: Albrecht Dürer, who has recently embraced Lutheranism, paints a diptych of John, Peter, Paul, and Mark and gives it to his native Nuremberg's town council, pairing the apostles with inscribed scripture warning against "human misguidance" as a public statement of Reformation belief.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Albrecht Dürer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The John and Peter panel of Dürer's The Four Apostles.

events.title: The Peace of Augsburg Divides the Empire's Faiths
events.body: Charles V's brother Ferdinand negotiates a settlement letting each prince choose Catholicism or Lutheranism as his territory's official faith, ending years of religious war within the empire under the principle that a ruler's religion determines his subjects' -- though it recognizes neither Calvinism nor the rights of individual dissenters.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by User:Michail, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The title page of the printed 1555 Peace of Augsburg.

events.title: Kepler Publishes His Laws of Planetary Motion in Prague
events.body: Working as imperial mathematician at Rudolf II's court in Prague, Johannes Kepler publishes Astronomia Nova, showing planets move in ellipses rather than perfect circles and overturning two thousand years of assumptions about how the heavens move.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Johannes Kepler, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The title page of Kepler's 1609 Astronomia Nova.

events.title: The Defenestration of Prague Ignites the Thirty Years' War
events.body: Protestant nobles storm Prague Castle and throw two Catholic royal governors and a secretary out of a third-story window in protest of Habsburg religious policy; all three survive the fall, but the act of open rebellion triggers a war that engulfs the empire for the next thirty years.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A contemporary broadsheet depicting the 1618 Defenestration of Prague.

events.title: Catholic Forces Crush the Bohemian Revolt at White Mountain
events.body: Imperial and Catholic League forces rout the army of Frederick V, the Protestant "Winter King" of Bohemia, outside Prague, ending the Bohemian phase of the Thirty Years' War, cementing Habsburg control over Bohemia, and setting off a brutal re-Catholicization of the kingdom.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Peter Snayers, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1630s painting of the Battle of White Mountain.

events.title: The Peace of Westphalia Ends the Thirty Years' War
events.body: Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück end thirty years of war that killed a large share of the empire's population, granting its territorial rulers greater religious and legal autonomy -- including recognition of Calvinism alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism -- while leaving the emperor's formal authority intact but increasingly nominal.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of the original treaty document, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A copy of the 1648 peace treaty signed at Osnabrück.

events.title: The Pragmatic Sanction Secures Maria Theresa's Succession
events.body: Emperor Charles VI issues the Pragmatic Sanction, decreeing that the Habsburg lands pass undivided to a daughter if he has no son, the legal groundwork that lets Maria Theresa inherit the Habsburg monarchy in 1740 and hold it together against rival claimants.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by User:Magellan, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Charles VI ratifying the Pragmatic Sanction's articles in 1723.

events.title: Charles VI Commissions the Karlskirche
events.body: Fulfilling a vow made during Vienna's last major plague outbreak, Emperor Charles VI commissions a grand domed church dedicated to the plague saint Charles Borromeo; architect Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach designs it, and his son completes it after his death, in 1737.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Thomas Ledl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Karlskirche in Vienna, lit by evening sun.

events.title: Joseph II Issues the Patent of Toleration
events.body: Emperor Joseph II grants Lutherans, Calvinists, and Orthodox Christians in Habsburg lands the right to worship privately and hold public office, a landmark Enlightenment-era retreat from centuries of enforced Catholic uniformity, though it still falls short of full religious equality.
events.imageAttribution: Document by Joseph II, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The first page of Joseph II's 1781 Patent of Toleration.

events.title: Francis II Dissolves the Holy Roman Empire
events.body: Facing an ultimatum from Napoleon, who has just organized sixteen German states into his own Confederation of the Rhine, Emperor Francis II abdicates the imperial throne and formally dissolves the Holy Roman Empire rather than let Napoleon claim the ancient title for himself.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Alphathon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Holy Roman Empire's territories in 1789, shortly before its dissolution.

name: Celts
summary: The Celts were a family of Iron Age peoples who shared related languages and a distinctive art style, spreading from a Central European heartland to dominate territory from Ireland to Anatolia at their height. Gaulish and British Celtic power was broken by Rome between the 1st century BC and 1st century AD, but Celtic culture endured and transformed in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and Brittany, producing a golden age of Christian monasticism and manuscript art before Viking pressure and Anglo-Norman expansion reshaped the Celtic-speaking world by the 11th century.
imageAttribution: Map by QuartierLatin1968, The Ogre, and Dbachmann, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map showing the Hallstatt-era Celtic homeland, the greatest extent of Celtic settlement around 275 BC, and areas where Celtic languages are still spoken today.

events.title: The Hallstatt Culture Emerges in Central Europe
events.body: Salt-mining elites in the Alpine region around Hallstatt, Austria develop a shared culture of ironworking, wagon burials, and richly decorated bronze and iron goods — the archaeological horizon historians now recognize as the earliest identifiable Celtic culture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Joanbanjo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A decorated bronze ceremonial axe from grave 504 at Hallstatt, Austria, dated to 800-750 BC.

events.title: The La Tène Style Redefines Celtic Art
events.body: Near Lake Neuchâtel, Celtic craftsmen begin fusing Mediterranean motifs with native curvilinear and animal-form designs into a new decorative style — later named for the La Tène site — that becomes the visual signature of Celtic art for the next four centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo of the Basse Yutz Flagons, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Basse-Yutz Flagons, a pair of bronze wine vessels from Lorraine, France, made around 450 BC in the earliest La Tène style.

events.title: Brennus and the Senones Sack Rome
events.body: A Senone war band under the chieftain Brennus annihilates a Roman army at the Allia River, then occupies and ransoms Rome itself — a humiliation traditionally dated to 390 BC in Roman sources, though modern scholarship places it closer to 387 BC.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Paul Joseph Jamin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Brenn et sa part du butin (1893), a painting by Paul Jamin imagining Brennus dividing the spoils taken from Rome.

events.title: The Battersea Shield Is Deposited in the Thames
events.body: Someone lowers a bronze parade shield decorated in flowing La Tène style into the River Thames near Battersea, likely as a votive offering — one of the finest surviving examples of British Celtic metalwork.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Geni, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Battersea Shield, a bronze-faced parade shield in La Tène style recovered from the River Thames.

events.title: Gauls Invade Greece, Turned Back at Thermopylae
events.body: A large Gallic army under another chieftain also named Brennus invades Greece and forces the same mountain pass where Leonidas once stood two centuries earlier, but a coalition of Greek states holds Thermopylae and the invaders are ultimately repelled short of their goal of plundering Delphi.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by antmoose, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Dying Gaul, a Roman marble copy of a Hellenistic bronze commemorating a Greek victory over Gallic invaders.

events.title: Celtic Settlers Found Galatia in Anatolia
events.body: After their defeat in Greece, surviving Gallic war bands cross into Anatolia at the invitation of a local king and, within two years, settle permanently in the highlands around modern Ankara, founding Galatia — a Celtic-speaking enclave that endures for centuries deep in Asia Minor.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Caliniuc, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Asia Minor's regions and settlements in the Greco-Roman period, showing Galatia in central Anatolia.

events.title: Bibracte Rises as a Fortified Gaulish Oppidum
events.body: The Aedui tribe fortifies a 200-hectare hilltop at Mont Beuvray with massive earthen ramparts, establishing Bibracte as one of Gaul's great oppida — the fortified proto-urban centers that anchor Gaulish political and economic life in the centuries before Roman conquest.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Iijjccoo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A surviving section of the fortification wall of Bibracte, the Aedui oppidum at Mont Beuvray.

events.title: The Gundestrup Cauldron Depicts Celtic Deities
events.body: Silversmiths craft an elaborately decorated ritual cauldron whose panels depict horned gods, warriors, and mythological beasts in Celtic style, before it is dismantled and buried in a Danish bog — the largest known surviving work of European Iron Age silverwork.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rosemania, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Gundestrup Cauldron, a richly decorated silver ritual vessel found in a Danish bog.

events.title: Caesar Defeats the Helvetii at Bibracte, Opening the Gallic Wars
events.body: When the Helvetii attempt to migrate through Gaul, Julius Caesar intercepts and crushes them near Bibracte in his first major battle in Gaul, a victory that draws him deeper into Gallic affairs and begins eight years of conquest.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Karl Jauslin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century illustration imagining the Helvetii chieftain Divico negotiating with Julius Caesar after the Battle of Bibracte.

events.title: The Aedui Uphold the Vergobret Magistracy
events.body: Among the Aedui and several neighboring tribes, a single annually elected chief magistrate called the vergobret holds executive and judicial power — barred by law from holding the office in consecutive years or serving alongside a relative, a built-in check against any one family seizing lasting control.
events.imageAttribution: Coin issued by the Lexovii, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons, via Bibliothèque nationale de France
events.imageDescription: A bronze coin of the Lexovii tribe naming the magistrate Cisiambos as vergobret.

events.title: Vercingetorix Is Proclaimed Leader of the United Gallic Tribes
events.body: After defeating Caesar at Gergovia, the Arverni noble Vercingetorix wins over the wavering Aedui and is acclaimed supreme commander of a pan-Gallic coalition at an assembly in Bibracte — the first time so many Gallic peoples unite under a single leader against Rome.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Bibliothèque nationale de France, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An electrum coin bearing a stylized portrait believed to depict Vercingetorix.

events.title: The Battle of Alesia Ends Gallic Independence
events.body: Caesar besieges Vercingetorix's army inside the hilltop oppidum of Alesia, building a double ring of fortifications to hold off both the trapped Gauls and a massive relief force, then starves the defenders into surrender — the last major battle of the Gallic Wars and the effective end of independent Gaul.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Benjamin Smith, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction of the Roman siege fortifications built around Alesia during the battle.

events.title: Rome Begins the Conquest of Britain
events.body: Emperor Claudius sends four legions across the Channel under Aulus Plautius, landing in Kent and beginning a campaign that brings most of southern Britain's Celtic tribes under Roman rule within a few decades.
events.imageAttribution: Map, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Roman military campaigns in Britain from AD 43 to 84.

events.title: Suetonius Paulinus Destroys the Druid Stronghold on Mona
events.body: While the Iceni and Trinovantes prepare to revolt, the Roman governor Suetonius Paulinus leads his legions against the island of Mona (Anglesey), a refuge for British rebels and a center of druidic religion, and destroys its defenders and sacred groves in a deliberate blow against Druidic influence in Britain.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Bernard de Montfaucon, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 18th-century engraving reproducing a Gallo-Roman relief at Autun depicting two druids.

events.title: Boudica Leads the Iceni in Revolt
events.body: Enraged after Roman officials seize her kingdom, flog her, and assault her daughters following her husband's death, the Iceni queen Boudica leads the Iceni and Trinovantes in revolt, burning Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium before the returning legions of Suetonius Paulinus crush her army in a decisive battle.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by John Opie, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Boadicea Haranguing the Britons (1793), a painting by John Opie imagining Boudica rallying her forces.

events.title: Ogham Script Emerges to Write Early Irish
events.body: Irish speakers devise Ogham, a distinctive alphabet of notches and lines carved along the edges of standing stones, to inscribe personal names and lineages — the earliest known written form of the Irish language.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jaqian, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An ogham stone from Rathass Church, Tralee, County Kerry, inscribed with notch-and-line script.

events.title: Saint Patrick Begins His Mission to Ireland
events.body: Patrick, a Romano-British former slave turned bishop, returns to Ireland as a missionary and spends decades founding churches across the island, becoming the central figure in Ireland's conversion to Christianity.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Andreas F. Borchert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A stained-glass window depicting Saint Patrick at Our Lady's Island, County Wexford.

events.title: Columba Founds Iona Abbey
events.body: The Irish monk Columba sails into exile with twelve companions and founds a monastery on the Scottish island of Iona, which grows into the launching point for Christian missions across Pictish and Scottish territory for centuries to come.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by J. R. Skelton, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An illustration of Columba confronting Bridei, King of the Picts, from a 1906 history of Scotland.

events.title: The Senchas Már Codifies Irish Brehon Law
events.body: Legal scholars compile the Senchas Már, a sprawling collection of forty-seven tracts covering everything from contracts and marriage to injury and beekeeping, into the single most authoritative text of Ireland's native Brehon legal tradition.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Andreas F. Borchert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of Cahermacnaghten in the Burren, County Clare, later home to a hereditary school of Brehon law.

events.title: The Book of Kells Is Illuminated
events.body: Columban monks, likely working across Iona and Kells, produce an elaborately illuminated Gospel book whose intricate interlace, spirals, and figural art represent the height of Insular Celtic manuscript art.
events.imageAttribution: Illuminated page from the Book of Kells, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Folio 32v of the Book of Kells, showing Christ Enthroned.

events.title: Kenneth MacAlpin Unites Picts and Scots as King of Alba
events.body: Kenneth MacAlpin, already king of Dál Riata, becomes king of the Picts as well, merging the two peoples into a single kingdom that Scottish tradition regards as the founding of Scotland, later cementing the union by moving Iona's relics and the coronation stone to the new royal centers of Dunkeld and Scone.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Stone of Scone set into the Coronation Chair at Westminster Abbey, the relic tied to the royal center Kenneth MacAlpin established at Scone.

events.title: The Battle of Clontarf
events.body: Brian Boru, High King of Ireland, defeats a coalition of the King of Leinster, the Norse-Irish King of Dublin, and Viking allies from Orkney and the Isle of Man near Dublin, breaking Norse political power in Ireland even as Brian himself is killed in the fighting.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Hugh Frazer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Battle of Clontarf (1826), an oil painting by Hugh Frazer depicting the 1014 battle.

events.title: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn Unites Wales
events.body: After decades of campaigning, Gruffudd ap Llywelyn becomes the only king in recorded history to bring the whole of Wales under a single ruler, governing from his court at Rhuddlan until English intervention ends his reign a few years later.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century engraving of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn from David Powel's Historie of Cambria.

events.title: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn Is Killed and Wales Fragments
events.body: Facing a joint English land and sea assault, Gruffudd is forced into retreat in Snowdonia, where his own men kill him and send his head to Harold Godwinson — ending the only period of unified Welsh rule and leaving Wales divided among rival princes just three years before the Norman Conquest reshapes power across Britain.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century engraving of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn from David Powel's Historie of Cambria.

name: Kingdom of Kush
summary: An ancient Nubian kingdom centered on the Nile south of Egypt, Kush rises after Egypt's New Kingdom withdraws from the region, later conquers and rules Egypt itself as the 25th Dynasty, and endures for centuries more from its southern capital at Meroe, known for its pyramids, ironworking, and a distinctive script, before fading amid internal strife and Aksumite pressure in the 4th century AD.
imageAttribution: Map by Lommes and पाटलिपुत्र, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map showing the Kushite heartland and the extent of the Kushite Empire during the 25th Dynasty, around 700 BCE.

events.title: Kush Regains Independence After Egyptian Withdrawal
events.body: As Egypt's New Kingdom empire disintegrates and its garrisons withdraw from Nubia, Kush re-emerges as an independent kingdom centered on the sacred mountain of Jebel Barkal near Napata, laying the foundation for over a thousand years of Kushite rule.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by LassiHU, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Jebel Barkal, the sacred mountain near Napata that anchored Kushite religion and kingship.

events.title: Alara Founds the Napatan Ruling Dynasty
events.body: Alara, later revered by his successors as the founder of their royal line, unifies Upper Nubia from the Third Cataract to Meroe and establishes Napata as Kush's religious capital; later Kushite kings invoke his name and pray for reigns as long as his.
events.imageAttribution: Drawing by Karl Richard Lepsius, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century facsimile of the royal cartouche of King Alara of Nubia.

events.title: Kashta Extends Kushite Influence into Thebes
events.body: King Kashta peacefully extends Kushite authority into Upper Egypt by installing his daughter Amenirdis I as heiress to the office of God's Wife of Amun at Thebes, a religious appointment that quietly cements Kushite influence over Egypt's most powerful priesthood.
events.imageAttribution: Ritual vessel by an unknown Egyptian artist, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bronze situla inscribed with the names of King Kashta and his daughter Amenirdis I.

events.title: Piye Conquers Lower Egypt and Founds the 25th Dynasty
events.body: Marching north from Napata, King Piye's forces take Herakleopolis, Hermopolis, and Memphis, and receive the submission of the Nile Delta's rulers, uniting Egypt and Nubia under Kushite rule as the 25th Dynasty; he commemorates the campaign on a victory stela at Jebel Barkal.
events.imageAttribution: Drawing by Auguste Mariette, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century drawing of Piye's victory stela recording the submission of Lower Egypt's rulers.

events.title: Shabaka Reunifies Egypt Under Kushite Rule
events.body: Shabaka, the third Kushite pharaoh of the 25th Dynasty, defeats the remaining Delta rivals and completes his predecessors' conquest, bringing all of Egypt from the Nile Delta to Nubia under a single Kushite crown.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by woodsboy2011, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A sphinx head bearing the likeness of King Shabaka.

events.title: Kushite Forces Aid Judah Against an Assyrian Siege
events.body: As King Sennacherib of Assyria besieges Jerusalem, a Kushite army marches to Judah's aid and meets the Assyrians near Eltekeh, a campaign later credited to Taharqa that becomes one of the most widely cited Kushite military interventions in the ancient Near East.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Tangopaso, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A statue of Taharqa displayed in the Louvre Museum.

events.title: The Shabaka Stone Preserves the Memphite Theology
events.body: Shabaka orders an ancient, damaged papyrus recording Egyptian creation theology copied onto a basalt slab, preserving what is now known as the Memphite Theology for later generations.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sanjay ach, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Shabaka Stone on display at the British Museum.

events.title: Taharqa's Building Program Reshapes Napata and Karnak
events.body: During his reign, Taharqa restores and expands temples across Egypt and Nubia, adding a great colonnaded kiosk at Karnak and raising the largest pyramid in the Nubian region at Nuri as his own tomb.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Hans Birger Nilsen, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The royal pyramids of the Napatan kings at Nuri, Sudan.

events.title: Esarhaddon's Assyrians Sack Memphis
events.body: Assyrian king Esarhaddon invades Egypt, storms Memphis, and captures Taharqa's family and court, forcing the Kushite pharaoh to flee south and breaking Kushite control over northern Egypt.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Assyrian relief depicting the storming of an Egyptian fortress on the Nile.

events.title: The Sack of Thebes Ends Kushite Rule in Egypt
events.body: Assyrian king Ashurbanipal's forces sack Thebes and rout the army of Tantamani, the last Kushite pharaoh of the 25th Dynasty, permanently ending Kushite control of Egypt and driving the dynasty's kings back to their Nubian heartland.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by tobeytravels, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A granite statue of King Tantamani, the last Kushite pharaoh of Egypt's 25th Dynasty.

events.title: Psamtik II Sacks Napata
events.body: Egyptian pharaoh Psamtik II leads an army deep into Nubia, storming Napata and smashing statues of its Kushite kings in retaliation for the earlier 25th Dynasty's rule over Egypt.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by OliBac, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A statue of Pharaoh Psamtik II on display at the Louvre-Lens.

events.title: Aspelta Relocates the Capital to Meroe
events.body: In the aftermath of Psamtik II's raid on Napata, King Aspelta shifts the kingdom's political center south to Meroe, a well-watered region rich in iron ore that offers safety from Egyptian attack and access to Red Sea trade routes.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jean-Pierre Dalbéra, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstructed statue of King Aspelta wearing an Egyptian-style headdress.

events.title: Royal Burials Complete the Shift to Meroe
events.body: By around 300 BC, Kushite kings and queens are buried exclusively at Meroe rather than Napata, a change scholars read as the monarchy finally breaking free of the Napatan priesthood's influence over royal succession.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Wufei07, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Pyramids N26 and N27 in the royal cemetery at Meroe.

events.title: The Meroitic Script Appears in Writing
events.body: Kush develops its own alphasyllabic script, Meroitic, in cursive and hieroglyphic forms; the earliest known inscription dates to this period, making it one of only a handful of indigenous writing systems in ancient Africa.
events.imageAttribution: Meroitic alphabet chart, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A chart comparing the Meroitic hieroglyphic and cursive scripts.

events.title: Amanirenas Leads Kush to War Against Rome
events.body: Queen Amanirenas leads a Kushite army into Roman Egypt, sacking Syene and toppling statues of Augustus; though a Roman counterattack under prefect Petronius drives her forces back, the resulting treaty exempts Kush from tribute and secures its independence from Rome.
events.imageAttribution: Drawing by Karl Richard Lepsius, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century facsimile of a relief from pyramid Bar. 4, identified by some scholars as the tomb of Amanirenas.

events.title: Kushites Bury a Trophy Head of Augustus
events.body: Kushite raiders carry off a bronze head from a statue of Augustus and bury it beneath the entrance steps of a Meroe temple, a symbolic act of subjugating the Roman emperor that preserves the sculpture intact for nearly two thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Aiwok, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The bronze Meroe Head of Augustus, now in the British Museum.

events.title: Natakamani and Amanitore Build the Lion Temple at Naqa
events.body: Co-rulers Natakamani and Amanitore, shown as equals in royal regalia on its walls, build the Temple of Apedemak at Naqa, dedicating it to Kush's lion-headed warrior god and blending Egyptian temple design with Nubian religious tradition.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by LassiHU, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Temple of Apedemak, the Lion Temple, at Naqa.

events.title: Aksumite Pressure and Internal Strife End the Kingdom of Kush
events.body: Weakened by Noba raids from the west and internal rebellion, Kush's capital at Meroe falls into decline; a Kushite king raises the region's last royal pyramid around this time, and an Aksumite military campaign under King Ezana delivers a blow from which ancient Nubia's kingdom never recovers.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin depicting King Ezana of Aksum, minted around 330–360 AD.

name: Phoenicia
summary: The Phoenicians were a network of independent Semitic city-states along the Levantine coast, rising to prominence after the Late Bronze Age collapse and led first by Byblos and then by Tyre, whose alliance with Solomon and expansion under Hiram I mark a golden age. Their invention of the alphabet -- adapted by the Greeks into their own -- and their colonization of the Mediterranean, culminating in the founding of Carthage in 814 BC, spread Phoenician trade and culture from Cyprus to Spain even as the homeland cities passed through Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian vassalage before Alexander stormed Tyre in 332 BC. Carthage carried the Phoenician (Punic) tradition forward as the dominant power of the western Mediterranean until Rome destroyed it in 146 BC, ending the civilization for good.
imageAttribution: Map by Kordas, based on Alvaro's work, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: Map showing the ancient Phoenician city-states along the Levantine coast.

events.title: Phoenician City-States Rise from the Bronze Age Collapse
events.body: As Egyptian and Hittite power recede amid the chaos of the Late Bronze Age collapse, the Canaanite coastal cities of Byblos, Sidon, and Tyre emerge as independent, prosperous city-states -- the beginning of what later writers call Phoenicia.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Orient (de.wikipedia), CC BY-SA 2.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Byblos, one of the oldest continuously inhabited Phoenician cities.

events.title: Ahiram's Sarcophagus Preserves the Mature Phoenician Alphabet
events.body: The inscribed sarcophagus of Byblos's King Ahiram carries the earliest lengthy example of the fully developed Phoenician alphabet, a 22-letter consonantal script that becomes the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, and Hebrew writing systems.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Matson Photo Service (1936), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The sarcophagus of Ahiram, King of Byblos, now in the Beirut National Museum.

events.title: Hiram I Unites Tyre's Twin Islands
events.body: King Hiram I joins Tyre's two islands with landfill, extends its harbor, and builds a royal palace and a temple to the god Melqart, launching roughly three decades of prosperity historians call Tyre's golden age.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Eyewatchlebanon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The traditional tomb of Hiram, King of Tyre, near Tyre in southern Lebanon.

events.title: Hiram I and Solomon Raise the Temple of Jerusalem
events.body: Hiram sends Tyrian architects, craftsmen, and cedar wood to help Solomon build the First Temple in Jerusalem, while the two kings jointly open a Red Sea trade route to the distant land of Ophir.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction of the floor plan of Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem.

events.title: Tyrian Settlers Found Kition on Cyprus
events.body: Colonists from Tyre establish Kition on Cyprus's southern coast, an early foothold that gives Phoenician traders access to the island's copper and a base for expansion further into the Mediterranean.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rjdeadly, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Remains of the Phoenician shipyard at Kition, on Cyprus.

events.title: Dido Founds Carthage
events.body: Fleeing her brother Pygmalion's tyranny in Tyre, the legendary queen Dido leads a band of settlers to the coast of North Africa and founds Carthage on land she buys by an oxhide's width, a trading post that grows into the greatest Phoenician city in the west.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by J. M. W. Turner, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: "Dido Building Carthage," Turner's 1815 painting of the legendary founding of the city.

events.title: Greeks Adapt the Phoenician Alphabet
events.body: Greek traders in close contact with Phoenician merchants borrow the Phoenician consonantal script and add vowel letters to fit their own language, a transformation that produces the Greek alphabet and, through it, the ancestor of most European writing systems.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Durutomo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Dipylon inscription, one of the earliest known examples of the Greek alphabet.

events.title: Assyria Extracts Tribute from Tyre and Byblos
events.body: Alarmed by Tiglath-Pileser III's crushing victory at Arpad, Tyre and Byblos begin paying tribute to Assyria rather than risk invasion, the start of two centuries in which Phoenicia's homeland cities keep their kings and trade but answer to a succession of foreign empires.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jastrow (2005), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Gypsum alabaster relief of Tiglath-Pileser III from his palace at Nimrud.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar's 13-Year Siege of Tyre Ends in Vassalage
events.body: After besieging Tyre for thirteen years without ever storming the city, Nebuchadnezzar II settles for a negotiated surrender that replaces its king with a Babylonian appointee, leaving Tyre intact but stripped of independence.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Stanley Llewelyn Wood, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A historical illustration of Tyre under siege by Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon.

events.title: Mago I Founds Carthage's Magonid Dynasty
events.body: Chosen as general after his predecessor is deposed for grasping at kingship, Mago I begins a dynasty of elected military leaders that transforms Carthage from a modest colony into the dominant Phoenician power of the western Mediterranean.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Javierfv1212, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The extent of the Carthaginian empire through the Punic Wars.

events.title: Carthage and the Etruscans Halt Greek Expansion at Alalia
events.body: An allied Carthaginian and Etruscan fleet fights Greek Phocaean colonists to a costly draw off Corsica, and though the Greeks win the immediate engagement, the battle stops their westward expansion and secures Carthaginian control of the western Mediterranean's trade routes.
events.imageAttribution: Map, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Map of the Tyrrhenian Sea showing the site of the Battle of Alalia off Corsica.

events.title: Eshmunazar II Builds the Temple of Eshmun
events.body: Sidon's King Eshmunazar II begins the sanctuary of Eshmun, the Phoenician god of healing, on a terrace above the Awali river; later kings expand it into what is today the best-preserved Phoenician religious site in Lebanon.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Elie+, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Throne of Astarte at the Temple of Eshmun, near Sidon.

events.title: The Phoenician Fleet Anchors Persia's Navy at Salamis
events.body: Phoenician ships make up the largest single contingent of Xerxes's fleet at the Battle of Salamis, and after the Greeks rout the crowded Persian line, Xerxes has several Phoenician captains beheaded for blaming the defeat on others.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Wilhelm von Kaulbach, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of the Battle of Salamis.

events.title: Carthage's Bid for Sicily Collapses at Himera
events.body: Carthaginian general Hamilcar lands a large army in Sicily to restore an ousted ally as tyrant of Himera, but Syracuse's Gelon and Agrigentum's Theron crush the invasion, crippling Carthaginian ambitions on the island for decades.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Giuseppe Sciuti, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of the Battle of Himera.

events.title: Tennes' Revolt Ends in the Burning of Sidon
events.body: King Tennes leads Sidon in revolt against Persian rule, then betrays the city to Artaxerxes III to save himself; Artaxerxes executes him anyway, and Sidon burns with, by ancient accounts, tens of thousands of its people trapped inside.
events.imageAttribution: Photo from the Bibliothèque nationale de France, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An ancient coin from Sidon minted under Tennes.

events.title: Alexander Storms Tyre After a Seven-Month Siege
