events.body: Alexander the Great builds a causeway out to island Tyre, breaches its walls after a seven-month siege, and in his fury has thousands of defenders killed or crucified and tens of thousands more sold into slavery, ending Phoenician political independence in the homeland for good.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by André Castaigne, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A naval action during Alexander's siege of Tyre, illustrated by André Castaigne.

events.title: Rome Wins the Battle of the Aegates, Ending the First Punic War
events.body: A Roman fleet destroys Carthage's last relief force off Sicily's Aegadian Islands, forcing Carthage to sue for peace, abandon Sicily, and pay a heavy war indemnity after 23 years of fighting.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sb2s3, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bronze warship ram recovered from the site of the Battle of the Aegates.

events.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps to Invade Italy
events.body: Carthaginian general Hannibal marches an army with war elephants over the Alps into Italy, opening the Second Punic War with a campaign of victories that keeps Roman legions on the defensive in Italy for over a decade.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Heinrich Leutemann, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century illustration of Hannibal's army crossing the Alps.

events.title: Rome Destroys Carthage, Ending Phoenician Civilization
events.body: After a brutal six-day final assault, Roman soldiers burn Carthage to the ground and kill most of its population, selling the roughly 50,000 survivors into slavery -- extinguishing the last independent Phoenician state and, with it, Phoenician civilization itself.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Harrias, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Carthage as it stood around 149 BC, on the eve of its destruction.

name: Ancient India
summary: Beginning with Chandragupta Maurya's conquest of Magadha and Ashoka's embrace of Buddhism after the brutal Kalinga War, ancient India's classical age unfolds through nearly five centuries of shifting successor kingdoms -- Shunga, Satavahana, Indo-Greek, and Kushan -- before the Gupta dynasty ushers in a golden age of Sanskrit literature, mathematics, and monumental architecture, ending amid Hunnic invasions and fragmentation around 550 CE.
imageAttribution: Photo by Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The North Gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, a Buddhist monument begun under the Maurya Empire.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
events.body: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nanda Empire and seizes Magadha, founding the Maurya Empire, which grows into the first empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent.
events.imageAttribution: Stamp design by Garudam, GODL-India, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 2001 Indian postage stamp depicting Chandragupta Maurya, founder of the Maurya Empire.

events.title: The Kalinga War
events.body: Ashoka's Maurya army conquers the independent kingdom of Kalinga in a brutal war; the scale of the bloodshed later drives Ashoka toward Buddhism and nonviolence.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bhajish Bharathan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ashoka's rock edicts at Dhauli, inscribed near the site of the Kalinga War.

events.title: Ashoka converts to Buddhism and issues his edicts
events.body: Remorseful after Kalinga, Ashoka embraces Buddhism and begins inscribing edicts of dharma on rocks and pillars across the empire, promoting nonviolence, religious tolerance, and public welfare.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sachin kumar tiwary, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: One of Ashoka's pillar edicts, at Lauriya Areraj in Bihar.

events.title: Ashoka commissions the Great Stupa at Sanchi
events.body: Ashoka has a hemispherical brick stupa built at Sanchi to house relics of the Buddha, the first monument on a hilltop site that grows into one of Buddhism's great architectural complexes.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Ashokan-era pillar standing at the Great Stupa site in Sanchi.

events.title: Pushyamitra Shunga overthrows the Maurya Empire
events.body: Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan military commander, assassinates the last Mauryan emperor Brihadratha during a troop review and founds the Shunga Empire in Magadha, ending a century of Mauryan rule.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Dhanadeva-Ayodhya inscription, a 1st-century BCE epigraph naming the Shunga dynasty.

events.title: Menander I converts to Buddhism
events.body: The Indo-Greek king Menander I, ruling from Sagala in the Punjab, embraces Buddhism after a recorded dialogue with the monk Nagasena, becoming a celebrated patron of the faith in the Hellenistic-influenced northwest.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin portrait of the Indo-Greek king Menander I.

events.title: The Satavahana dynasty is founded
events.body: Simuka establishes the Satavahana dynasty in the Deccan, filling the power vacuum left by Maurya collapse and building a long-lived kingdom that dominates central and southern India for over three centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Uploadalt, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of the later Satavahana king Vashishtiputra Sri Satakarni, photographed at the British Museum.

events.title: Ornamental gateways rise at the Sanchi Stupa
events.body: Under Satavahana patronage, elaborately carved stone gateways depicting scenes from the Buddha's life are added to the Great Stupa at Sanchi, replacing its simpler earlier entrances.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The carved Eastern Gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi.

events.title: Kujula Kadphises unifies the Kushan Empire
events.body: Kujula Kadphises unites the five Yuezhi tribes of Bactria under his rule, founding the Kushan Empire, which soon expands south across the Hindu Kush into the Indian subcontinent.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by Classical Numismatic Group, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A tetradrachm coin of the Kushan king Kujula Kadphises.

events.title: Kanishka becomes Kushan emperor
events.body: Kanishka takes the Kushan throne and rules from twin capitals at Purushapura and Mathura, presiding over the empire's territorial and commercial peak along the Silk Road.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gold coin of Kanishka, held at the British Museum.

events.title: Kanishka convenes a great Buddhist council in Kashmir
events.body: Kanishka sponsors a gathering of Buddhist scholars in Kashmir, remembered in tradition as the Fourth Buddhist Council, that produces authoritative commentaries on Buddhist scripture and helps carry Buddhism along Central Asian trade routes.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain (Peshawar Museum, 1930), via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Buddhist sculptural group from the Peshawar Museum, from the Gandhara region patronized under Kanishka.

events.title: The Gandhara school of Greco-Buddhist art flourishes
events.body: Sculptors in Gandhara, working under Kushan patronage, blend Hellenistic artistic technique inherited from the region's Greek-ruled past with Buddhist subject matter, producing some of the first anthropomorphic images of the Buddha.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by World Imaging, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1st-century Gandharan sculpture of the Buddha in Greco-Buddhist style.

events.title: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire
events.body: Chandragupta I is crowned Maharajadhiraja, marking the start of the Gupta Empire and the Gupta calendar era; his marriage to the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi strengthens the new dynasty's standing in Magadha.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Uploadalt, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gold coin depicting Chandragupta I and Queen Kumaradevi.

events.title: Samudragupta expands the Gupta Empire
events.body: Samudragupta campaigns across northern and southern India, uprooting rival kings and extending Gupta authority from the Himalayas toward the Deccan; his conquests are recorded on the Allahabad Pillar inscription.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta.

events.title: Chandragupta II defeats the Western Kshatrapas
events.body: Chandragupta II conquers the Saka Western Kshatrapas of Gujarat and Malwa, giving the Gupta Empire access to the western coast's sea trade and bringing it to its greatest territorial extent.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of Chandragupta II depicted on horseback.

events.title: Sanskrit literature flourishes under Chandragupta II
events.body: The poet-playwright Kalidasa, widely regarded as ancient India's greatest Sanskrit writer, is thought to have composed his major works during Chandragupta II's reign, part of a broader flowering of Sanskrit literature and drama under Gupta patronage.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by William Douglas Almond, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An early-20th-century illustration imagining Kalidasa composing verse.

events.title: The Iron Pillar is forged under Chandragupta II
events.body: Metalworkers cast a 7-metre iron pillar honoring Chandragupta II, using a corrosion-resistant alloy that keeps the column virtually rust-free some sixteen centuries later -- a landmark of Gupta-era metallurgy.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mark A. Wilson, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Iron Pillar, now standing in the Qutb complex in Delhi.

events.title: Kumaragupta I founds Nalanda
events.body: Kumaragupta I endows a monastery at Nalanda that grows into the ancient world's foremost center of learning, drawing students and scholars from across Asia to study Buddhist philosophy alongside grammar, medicine, and logic.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Odantapuribs, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of Temple No. 3 at the Nalanda archaeological site.

events.title: Skandagupta repels a Hunnic invasion
events.body: Skandagupta defeats an invasion by Hunnic raiders, probably the Kidarites, restoring Gupta military prestige at the start of his reign even as the empire's northwestern frontier comes under growing pressure.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of Skandagupta, shown holding a bow and arrow.

events.title: Aryabhata completes the Aryabhatiya
events.body: Working at Kusumapura, Aryabhata completes the Aryabhatiya, a landmark treatise that lays out a decimal place-value number system, calculates pi to four decimal places, and explains solar and lunar eclipses through the Earth's rotation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Cpjha13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern statue of Aryabhata in Bihar.

events.title: Mihirakula's Huna forces overrun Gupta's northwest
events.body: The Alchon Hun king Mihirakula conquers Sindh and pushes into Punjab and Kashmir, breaking Gupta control over the subcontinent's northwest and accelerating the empire's fragmentation.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A numismatic portrait of the Alchon Hun king Mihirakula.

events.title: The Gupta Empire fragments and falls
events.body: Weakened by decades of Hunnic incursions and the rise of regional rivals such as Yashodharman, the Gupta Empire fades into a scatter of successor kingdoms; Vishnugupta, the last recognized ruler of the main line, issues his final inscription around this time.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Koba-chan, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the Gupta Empire's extent around 420 CE, before its later fragmentation.

name: Israel and Judah
summary: The Israelite kingdoms rise from a loose tribal confederation into a united monarchy under Saul, David, and Solomon, then split into a northern Kingdom of Israel and a southern Kingdom of Judah. Israel falls to Assyria in 720 BCE and Judah falls to Babylon in 587 BCE, ending in exile until Cyrus's edict permits the Jewish captives to return.
imageAttribution: Map by Edward Weller, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A 19th-century map depicting the ancient kingdoms of Judah and Israel.

events.title: Saul Becomes the First King of Israel
events.body: The tribal confederation of Israel unites under a single monarch for the first time as Saul is anointed king, traditionally placed in the late 11th century BCE and ending the era of the judges.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Ernst Josephson, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1878 oil painting depicting King Saul.

events.title: David Captures Jerusalem and Makes It His Capital
events.body: David storms the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem and installs it as his new capital, then brings the Ark of the Covenant into the city, binding Israelite kingship to Jerusalem for the rest of its history.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Gerard van Honthorst, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1622 painting of King David playing the harp.

events.title: Solomon Succeeds David as King
events.body: Solomon inherits the throne from his father David and consolidates the united kingdom's wealth and influence, presiding over what tradition remembers as Israel's golden age.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Simeon Solomon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1872–1874 painting portraying King Solomon.

events.title: Solomon Completes the First Temple in Jerusalem
events.body: After seven years of construction using cedar and craftsmen supplied by Hiram I of Tyre, Solomon dedicates the First Temple in Jerusalem as the central sanctuary of Israelite worship, housing the Ark of the Covenant.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by François Vatable, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century engraving reconstructing the appearance of Solomon's Temple.

events.title: Solomon Fortifies Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer
events.body: Solomon rebuilds and fortifies a chain of administrative and military cities across the kingdom, including Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer, while dividing the realm into twelve districts to supply his court.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Golf Bravo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ancient six-chambered city gate at Tel Megiddo.

events.title: The Queen of Sheba Visits Solomon's Court
events.body: According to the biblical narrative, the Queen of Sheba travels to Jerusalem to test Solomon's wisdom with hard questions and returns south laden with gifts, a story later retold across Jewish, Christian, Islamic, and Ethiopian tradition.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Edward Slocombe, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1907 painting of the Queen of Sheba.

events.title: The United Monarchy Splits into Israel and Judah
events.body: After Solomon's death, his son Rehoboam's harsh rule triggers a revolt led by Jeroboam; ten northern tribes break away to form the Kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam, leaving Rehoboam with the southern Kingdom of Judah centered on Jerusalem.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Tobias Schäfer 87, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the kingdoms of Israel and Judah after their division.

events.title: Jeroboam Sets Up Rival Shrines at Bethel and Dan
events.body: To keep his new subjects from making pilgrimage to Jerusalem's temple, Jeroboam I erects golden calf shrines at Bethel and Dan, establishing rival cult centers that mark the religious break between Israel and Judah.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Jean-Honoré Fragonard, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 18th-century painting of Jeroboam offering sacrifice to an idol.

events.title: Pharaoh Shoshenq I Raids Israel and Judah
events.body: Egyptian Pharaoh Shoshenq I campaigns through the Levant and records dozens of captured towns in Israel and Judah on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, the earliest Egyptian inscription to corroborate the biblical account of the two kingdoms.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Markh, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Bubastite Portal at Karnak, inscribed with Shoshenq I's list of conquered towns.

events.title: Omri Founds Samaria as Israel's New Capital
events.body: King Omri purchases a hill in the central highlands and builds Samaria, a fortified new capital that becomes the political and cultural center of the northern Kingdom of Israel for over a century and a half.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Guillaume Roullié, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century printed portrait of King Omri.

events.title: Ahab Joins the Coalition Against Assyria at Qarqar
events.body: King Ahab of Israel contributes chariots and infantry to an eleven-king Levantine coalition that halts Shalmaneser III's advance at Qarqar, an engagement recorded on Shalmaneser's own monument rather than in the Bible.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Yuber, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Kurkh stela of Shalmaneser III recording the Battle of Qarqar.

events.title: Elijah Confronts the Prophets of Baal at Mount Carmel
events.body: During Ahab's reign, the prophet Elijah challenges 450 prophets of Baal to a sacrifice contest on Mount Carmel; when fire falls only on his own altar, the assembled Israelites affirm Yahweh as their God and Elijah has the Baal prophets put to death.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Giovanni Girolamo Savoldo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century painting of the prophet Elijah fed by a raven.

events.title: Jehu Purges the House of Ahab and Pays Tribute to Assyria
events.body: Jehu seizes the throne of Israel by killing King Jehoram and the rest of Ahab's dynasty, then submits to Assyrian power; Shalmaneser III commemorates his tribute on the Black Obelisk, the only surviving portrait of an Israelite king.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Steven G. Johnson, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Jehu of Israel depicted bowing before Shalmaneser III on the Black Obelisk.

events.title: The Priest Jehoiada Overthrows Queen Athaliah
events.body: Six years after Athaliah seized Judah's throne and promoted Baal worship following her son's death, the priest Jehoiada leads a coup that kills her and crowns the boy king Joash, restoring the Davidic line.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Guillaume Roullié, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century printed portrait of Queen Athaliah.

events.title: Ahaz Buys Assyrian Help Against the Syro-Ephraimite Coalition
events.body: When Israel and Aram-Damascus besiege Jerusalem to force Judah into an anti-Assyrian alliance, King Ahaz instead pays homage to Tiglath-Pileser III with treasure from the Temple, turning back the invasion but making Judah an Assyrian tributary.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Guillaume Roullié, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century printed portrait of King Ahaz.

events.title: Assyria Conquers Samaria and Ends the Kingdom of Israel
events.body: After a three-year siege begun by Shalmaneser V and completed by Sargon II, Samaria falls and the Assyrians deport thousands of Israelites to Mesopotamia and Media, dispersing the ten northern tribes and ending the Kingdom of Israel.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Joelholdsworth, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the Assyrian deportation of Israelites from the conquered Kingdom of Israel.

events.title: Hezekiah Centralizes Worship at the Jerusalem Temple
events.body: Hezekiah purges the Temple of idols, tears down the high places used for sacrifice across Judah, and destroys the bronze serpent Nehushtan, concentrating Yahwistic worship at Jerusalem in the wake of Israel's fall to Assyria.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by David Castor of a 17th-century painting, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century painting of King Hezekiah in Sankta Maria kyrka, Åhus, Sweden.

events.title: Hezekiah Carves the Siloam Tunnel to Secure Jerusalem's Water
events.body: Anticipating an Assyrian siege, Hezekiah has workers cut a 533-meter tunnel through bedrock to channel the Gihon Spring into the city, and the two crews who dug from opposite ends leave a Hebrew inscription describing the moment they met in the middle.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Wikikati, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A replica of the Siloam inscription describing the tunnel's construction.

events.title: Sennacherib Besieges Jerusalem but Fails to Take It
events.body: Assyrian king Sennacherib overruns Judah's fortified cities and traps Hezekiah 'like a bird in a cage' in Jerusalem, but withdraws without capturing the city, an outcome the Bible credits to divine intervention and one that Assyrian records omit entirely.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Lior Golgher, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Remains of the broad wall Hezekiah built in Jerusalem to defend against Sennacherib's siege.

events.title: Manasseh Supplies Forced Labor to Assyria's Building Projects
events.body: As a loyal Assyrian vassal, Manasseh of Judah is listed among twenty-two kings required to furnish materials and labor for Esarhaddon's construction projects, and later assists Ashurbanipal's campaign against Egypt.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Guillaume Roullié, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 16th-century printed portrait of King Manasseh.

events.title: Josiah's Reforms Follow the Discovery of the Book of the Law
events.body: While renovating the Temple, high priest Hilkiah finds a scroll of the Law; after having it authenticated, Josiah purges Baal worship, destroys shrines from Beersheba to Bethel, and restores the Passover, the most sweeping religious reform in Judah's history.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by David Castor of a 17th-century painting, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century painting of King Josiah in Sankta Maria kyrka, Åhus, Sweden.

events.title: Josiah Dies Opposing Egypt at the Battle of Megiddo
events.body: When Pharaoh Necho II marches north to aid the last Assyrian remnants against Babylon, Josiah blocks his passage at Megiddo and is killed in the battle, ending Judah's brief independence and reducing it to an Egyptian vassal.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Keith Schengili-Roberts, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bronze kneeling statuette of Pharaoh Necho.

events.title: Babylon Defeats Egypt at Carchemish
events.body: Nebuchadnezzar II crushes the Egyptian army and its remaining Assyrian allies at Carchemish, ending Egyptian power in the Levant and bringing Judah, recently Necho's vassal, under Babylonian domination instead.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from Hutchinson's History of the Nations, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1915 illustration depicting the Battle of Carchemish.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar Deports King Jehoiachin to Babylon
events.body: Nebuchadnezzar II besieges Jerusalem after Jehoiakim's rebellion, and when the young Jehoiachin surrenders, deports him along with 3,000 Judeans to Babylon, installing his uncle Zedekiah as a puppet king in his place.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by James Tissot, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A painting depicting Judean captives being marched into exile.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar Destroys Jerusalem and the First Temple
events.body: After a 30-month siege breaks Zedekiah's revolt, Babylonian forces raze Jerusalem's walls, burn the First Temple, and deport most of the remaining population, ending the Kingdom of Judah's four centuries of independence.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Michel Wolgemut and Wilhelm Pleydenwurff, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A woodcut from the 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle depicting the destruction of Jerusalem.

events.title: The Assassination of Gedaliah Ends Local Judean Rule
events.body: Babylon's appointed governor Gedaliah is murdered at Mizpah by a rival claimant to the Davidic throne; fearing reprisal, the remaining Judeans flee to Egypt, extinguishing the last local government in the land and leading later Jews to mark the date with the Fast of Gedaliah.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Gebhard Fugel, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A painting evoking the Judean exiles' lament in Babylon.

events.title: Babylon Releases Jehoiachin from Prison
events.body: On ascending the Babylonian throne, Evil-Merodach frees the exiled Jehoiachin after 37 years of captivity, seats him above the other exiled kings, and grants him a regular allowance, a small easing of conditions recorded both in the Bible and on Babylonian ration tablets.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Scallaham, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Babylonian ration tablet listing provisions for Jehoiachin and his sons.

events.title: Cyrus's Edict Ends the Babylonian Exile
events.body: After conquering Babylon, Cyrus the Great issues an edict permitting the exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, closing the Babylonian captivity and opening the Second Temple period.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Prioryman, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Cyrus Cylinder, recording Cyrus's policy of restoring displaced peoples and temples.

name: Minoan & Mycenaean
summary: The Minoan civilization on Crete and the Mycenaean civilization on the Greek mainland were the Aegean world's first major Bronze Age societies, linked by trade, art, and eventually conquest. Minoan Crete built the Mediterranean's earliest palaces and a far-reaching maritime trading network, while Mycenaean Greece rose through a warrior aristocracy, fortified citadels, and Linear B administration. Volcanic disaster, internal upheaval, and the wider Late Bronze Age Collapse ended both civilizations, ushering in the Greek Dark Ages by 1100 BC.
imageAttribution: Photo by Joyofmuseums, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Lion Gate, the monumental entrance to the Mycenaean citadel at Mycenae.

events.title: Bronze Age Settlement Begins on Crete
events.body: Farming communities on Crete enter the Bronze Age, laying the groundwork for what will become Europe's first major civilization. Early Minoan society develops metalworking, seafaring, and the trade networks that later palaces will build on.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Bibi Saint-Pol, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Minoan-era Crete showing its major settlements and palace sites.

events.title: First Minoan Palaces Built at Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia
events.body: Growing populations on Crete build the island's first monumental palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia, marking the start of the Old Palace period. These centers organize agriculture, craft production, and long-distance trade under a shared Minoan culture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Dougal96, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The reception courtyard at the palace of Knossos, where Minoan rulers received visitors.

events.title: Earthquake Destroys the Old Palaces; Knossos Rebuilt
events.body: A powerful earthquake, or series of them, levels Crete's Old Palaces around 1700 BC. Knossos and the other centers are rebuilt on a grander scale, opening the Neopalatial period, the height of Minoan art and architecture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Frederic Boissonnas, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The north entrance of the rebuilt palace at Knossos.

events.title: Grave Circle A Marks the Rise of Mycenae's Warrior Elite
events.body: A new royal burial ground at Mycenae, Grave Circle A, is stocked with gold masks, weapons, and jewelry, revealing a wealthy and increasingly powerful warrior aristocracy on the Greek mainland. The roughly 15 kilograms of gold buried across its shaft graves signal Mycenae's rise as a major Aegean power.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Andreas Trepte, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Grave Circle A and the citadel entrance at Mycenae.

events.title: Snake Goddess Figurines Placed in Knossos's Temple Repositories
events.body: Faience figurines of women holding snakes are deposited in stone-lined "Temple Repositories" at Knossos. Long treated as a symbol of Minoan religion, their exact meaning, whether goddesses, priestesses, or something else entirely, remains debated among scholars.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by C messier, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: One of the Minoan snake goddess figurines excavated at Knossos in 1903.

events.title: Thera Eruption Devastates Akrotiri
events.body: A massive volcanic eruption on Thera (Santorini) buries the town of Akrotiri in ash and reshapes the island, one of the largest eruptions in human history. The Minoans recover and enter their cultural peak in the decades after, though the eruption's role in the civilization's later decline is still debated.
events.imageAttribution: Satellite photo by NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A satellite image of Santorini, the caldera left by the Minoan eruption.

events.title: Bull-Leaping Fresco Captures a Minoan Ritual
events.body: Palace artists at Knossos paint the Bull-Leaping Fresco, showing acrobats vaulting over a charging bull. The scene captures a ceremonial sport thought to carry religious significance, though its exact purpose is still unclear a century after its discovery.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Gleb Simonov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The restored Bull-Leaping Fresco from the palace at Knossos.

events.title: Mycenaeans Take Control of Knossos
events.body: Widespread destruction sweeps across Crete's palaces around 1450 BC, sparing only Knossos, which comes under Mycenaean Greek control. Linear B, an early form of Greek, replaces the still-undeciphered Linear A as the script of palace administration.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Chris 73, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The throne hall at Knossos, used during the Mycenaean administration of the palace.

events.title: Fire Destroys Knossos, Ending Minoan Palatial Rule
events.body: A fire destroys the palace at Knossos around 1350 BC, ending its role as a Mycenaean administrative center and closing the palatial era of Minoan civilization. The blaze bakes and preserves hundreds of Linear B tablets, offering a snapshot of the palace's final administration.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Lapplaender, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ruins of the upper floor of the palace of Knossos, with Mount Giouchtas in the background.

events.title: Uluburun Shipwreck Reveals Bronze Age Trade Networks
events.body: A merchant ship sinks off the coast of Uluburun carrying copper, tin, glass, ivory, and luxury goods gathered from across the Mediterranean and Near East, likely bound for a Mycenaean palace. The wreck's cargo shows how deeply Mycenaean Greece was woven into Late Bronze Age royal trade and gift exchange.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Martin Bahmann, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An artifact recovered from the Uluburun shipwreck.

events.title: Treasury of Atreus Built at Mycenae
events.body: Mycenaean builders complete the Treasury of Atreus, a monumental tholos tomb with a corbelled dome roughly 14.5 meters wide. It remains the largest dome of its kind built anywhere for over a thousand years, until Roman engineers surpass it.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Ken Russell Salvador, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The corbelled entrance passage of the Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae.

events.title: Bronze Age Collapse Reaches the Mycenaean Mainland
events.body: Palatial centers across the Greek mainland, including Mycenae and Tiryns, suffer earthquakes and destruction as the wider Late Bronze Age Collapse sweeps the eastern Mediterranean. Trade networks fracture and the palace economies that sustained Mycenaean power begin to unravel.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Alexikoua, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of invasions, destructions, and population movements during the Bronze Age Collapse.

events.title: Legendary Fall of Troy
events.body: Ancient chronographers, including Eratosthenes, date the fall of Troy to around 1184 BC, the climax of the Trojan War later immortalized in Homer's epics. Archaeologists have found a real destruction layer at Troy from around this time, though how closely it matches the legend is still debated.
events.imageAttribution: Painting attributed to the Sosias Painter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A red-figure vase painting of Achilles tending to the wounded Patroclus, a scene from the Trojan War.

events.title: Palace of Nestor Burns, Preserving Pylos's Linear B Archive
events.body: Fire destroys the Palace of Nestor at Pylos, but the same heat bakes and preserves over a thousand Linear B tablets, the largest such archive found in Greece. Among the records are some of the earliest written references to Greek gods, including Poseidon, Zeus, Hera, and Dionysus.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Alun Salt, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Remains of a bathing structure at the Palace of Nestor in Pylos.

events.title: Mycenaean Civilization Ends
events.body: By 1100 BC, the last Mycenaean palatial centers are abandoned and Linear B writing falls out of use, closing the Aegean Bronze Age. The centuries that follow, marked by smaller, isolated communities, become known as the Greek Dark Ages.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by David Monniaux, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ruins of the citadel at Mycenae.
